utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry and Mr. Huber, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic. I'm representing Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Along with me here is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm Howard Morrison. I appear with Madam Buturovic for the defendant Mucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the further appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo. I represented Mr. Hazim Delic, together with my colleague, Mr. Tom Moran, attorney at law from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Nancy Boler, and together with lead counsel Cynthia McMurrey, who is not present in the courtroom today, we represent Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. We are still on with Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to call Mr. Nebojsa Manigodjic to the courtroom. The Defence has completed its examination-in-chief, and I believe it's my colleague turn now from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Niemann. Kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manigodjic.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you some questions about what you were saying in your evidence. Did you say that you lived in Konjic up until the war and then went to Jablanica or did you always live in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: I always lived in Jablanica, and my family has been living in Jablanica for 250 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it then that your business extended into areas such as in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very narrow area, and Jablanica is only, maybe, 40 kilometres away from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that you visited Mr. Delalic in Vienna, and you saw him in the club there. Do you remember the name of the club?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: It was the club that gathered friends of Bosnia. This was the basis for their getting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know whether or not Mr. Delalic had any connection to that club, other than being just a member of it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: I did not have any specific information that he was. As I told you, people who gathered in that club, as far as I learned, in Vienna, were people from Jablanica, whom I knew and whom I had to see on that occasion. So that was the reason of my going there. On that occasion, I also met with Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay with Mr. Delalic on that occasion at his home?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, I stayed both at Mr. Delalic's home, maybe for one day, and the rest of the time I spent with other people from Jablanica. People are curious. They were wanting to know how things were at home, so I had to spend some time with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me a moment. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination? Have you any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are discharged. You may go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I call the witness Ibrahim Cilic to take the stand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour? JUDGE-KARIBI-WHYTE: You may, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please introduce yourself by stating your full name?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: My name is Ibrahim Cilic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, what is your ethnic background and what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak by ethnic background, and I'm a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, are you related to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Not directly, but I married the daughter of his brother Dzafer, his niece. I guess you can call it a family relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: I've known Mr. Delalic since 1985. I married Almina that year. She is the daughter of his late brother Dzafer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you meet with Mr. Zejnil Delalic frequently?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. We met on a number of occasions after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, do you know what kind of family Mr. Delalic is from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic comes from a large and poor family. He has a lot of brothers and sisters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, when he became a successful businessman, do you know whether he helped members of his family?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As far as I know, he was quite a successful businessman in Germany, and he helped his family, both his close family and his large family. I know that he helped, personally, my wife, his niece Almina. He paid for her education in Sarajevo, and he also helped her brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you and your wife feel gratitude towards Mr. Zejnil Delalic because of his attitude towards her?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Yes, because of his attitude, not only towards her, but towards the whole family in general. We were really thankful to Mr. Zejnil Delalic, and we also decided that we should help his family now that he was in trouble.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what I would like to ask you. Do you know where Mr. Delalic's children and his wife live at the moment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic's children are living currently in Belgrade, and they come, from time to time, to their family house in Konjic. I saw them there on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, do you know who supported the children and the ex-wife of Mr. Zejnil Delalic before he was detained?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Before Mr. Zejnil Delalic was detained, he personally supported his children and his wife. As far as I know, he held his family in very high regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, you said, as a sign of gratitude for Mr. Delalic did for your wife when she was in need, that you decided to help his family now. Tell us, what do you do exactly in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly as you said, we decided to help his family. Now I have a private business in Jablanica, and I have certain means and resources to help them now that they are in a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, do you know whether, throughout this period, this year or last year, whether Gordana Delalic, the wife of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, came to Konjic with her children. If she did so, could you tell us how she was accepted, how she was received, by your family and the town of Konjic in general?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: His wife used to come to their family house in Konjic, and me and my wife, we would personally go there to pay them a visit in their family house, and she was received very well by citizens of Konjic in general. When we went there to that house, we saw people from all ethnic backgrounds in their house, lots of their friends who never stopped being their friends, people who were interested in his situation and people who came to The Hague. She was received very well by all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, since you are related to Mr. Zejnil Delalic, could you tell us whether you know that Zejnil Delalic, whenever he could, helped people who were not members of his family?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that. He helped a lot of citizens from Jablanica. Whenever he was asked for help, he would gladly do so, either financially or in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, did you ever notice Mr. Delalic having a different attitude towards members of other ethnic communities, or did he have friends from all ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any difference in attitude, any difference in his behaviour. He was very well-respected by anyone as an honest man, a highly moral person. Mr. Delalic was thought to be a cosmopolitan, and he never distinguished amongst people according to their nationality, religion, of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with him on a couple of occasions in Jablanica during the war? If you did, did you notice that he had changed in any way, that he had changed his attitude in that respect?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: I met him only once during the war in passing. Actually, I just saw him, and I didn't have an opportunity to talk to him. At that time, we were all running around. We had lots of obligations, but I didn't notice any change in his behaviour. On the contrary, he was esteemed by everyone in the community.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My last question for you, Mr. Cilic, when Zejnil Delalic left the area in late 1992, the Court knows, and you as a member of his family probably also know, that he was a victim of very intensive propaganda. He was accused of being a member of KOS. What I'd like to know is whether Zejnil Delalic, in spite of that, continued helping people who were in trouble. Do you know of any specific example as regards Jablanica where he sent some assistance, some aid, to the town in general?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that. I know that he helped people in Ostrozac and Jablanica at that time. My mother-in-law spent some time in the area after the conflict with the HVO, and I know that he even sent some money on one occasion for the flour to be purchased for the town of Jablanica in general. At that time, both Muslims and Serbs lived in Jablanica. It was a mixed community. He helped individuals in general, if anyone needed, for example, medical treatment and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cilic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: None for Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: None from the Defence of Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have the Prosecutor any questions for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, did you ever hear of Mr. Delalic being referred to by a nickname of Pera, P-E-R-A?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM CILIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Call your other witness. You are discharged. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I call the next witness for the Defence, Mr. Branko Tomann.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Will you please introduce yourself by giving the Court your full name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: My name is Branko Tomann, and I would like to extend my greetings to all the ladies and gentlemen present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomann, will you please tell us, what is your ethnic background and what is your citizenship?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I'm an Austrian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomann, what are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I am a medical technician. I'm a specialist in radiology, and I also graduated in Slavic studies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also engage in any sports activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Until the age of 50, that is, until 1990, I was a referee in the Soccer Association of Austria. After 1994, I joined the Football Association of Bosniaks in Austria. At first, I was a referee, and then I became an instructor who controls the quality of the work of referees. I'm also a member of the Football Association.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As everybody can notice, as an Austrian citizen, you speak Serbo-Croatian very well. You said you studied Slavic studies, but can you tell us where you were born and did you live in Bosnia-Herzegovina at any time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I forgot my Serbo-Croatian a little bit, but I was born in Bosnia and I lived there for 18 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You lived in Bosnia as an ethnic minority, an Austrian in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I lived there. My grandfather was a high ranking officer in the Austrian army, so my mother tongue is really Austrian, but we got along very well with people in Bosnia, and I still have affection for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tomann, how long have you known Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I met Mr. Delalic sometime in mid-1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomann, when did you meet Mr. Delalic and on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: This is, I don't know, maybe a longer or a shorter story. When I take the tram to go to work in the 17th district in Vienna, in Tabergasstrasse 15, once as I was riding on the tram, I saw a sign saying Gemeinschaft BiH and let me give you a translation. It was actually an association of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's where I met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw this sign in the middle of 1993 and that you met him sometime in mid-1994. Did you go in to the premises of this association and did you join this association as an Austrian?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Until 1990, as a person who used to live in Yugoslavia, I associated with all nations and minorities from the territory of the former Yugoslavia. When these quarrels started over there, I stopped going to all restaurants or associations or clubs, because I did not know who was behind it all. Maybe there were some extremists there, some nationalists there. So I decided not to pursue this, and then sometime, I think it was in April 1994, an art show opening was going to take place from well-known painters from Serbia, Bosnia, Macedonia, Croatia, and the poster said that all proceeds from this art exhibit were going to be sent as humanitarian help for children in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this announcement for the art exhibit with participation of artists from all over the Yugoslavia, did that make you decide to go there and join this association?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I was hesitating, but there was this lady, Madam Biserka, and there was a well-known painter from Belgrade who managed to get out and bring his work there. I thought that all this showed some kind of solidarity. I thought, "I'm Austrian. I speak German. Nobody knows me. I will not show that I can speak Serbo-Croatian, so I will show up. I will go there."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this when you first met Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Yes. After awhile, there were speeches. There were addresses by invitees, and after a number of things, I finally met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delalic also address the invited guests there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: At the opening, Mr. Simon Wiesenthal spoke, and I was very glad when I saw it in the catalogue, and I believe you may have the catalogue, first it was Mr. Wiesenthal that mentioned that this was for peace and against fascism. So Mr. Wiesenthal spoke, and then the deputy minister -- I'm thinking in German, so give me a moment, please, yes, Alois Mock, the deputy foreign minister who is also a member of this club, as well as a Mr. Simon Wiesenthal is also an honorary member of this club. They talked about the suffering of children in Bosnia. There was people there from different humanitarian organisations, there was a press conference. The whole cultural elite of Austria showed up. The editor in chief of the Sarajevo newspaper, Sergej Princip, who is a Serb, also spoke there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delalic also speak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic interpreted. At that time, I, actually, didn't know that this was Mr. Delalic. I just saw a nice man, a bit corpulent. He was interpreting. Afterwards, he spoke too. I can only recall one small part. He said, "Why are we here? They imposed unofficial borders to us, but the humanitarian and the human heart are larger than all these artificial borders, and we are here to prove that we are all together."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At this art opening, when you heard Delalic speak, how did you experience Zejnil Delalic? What did you think of him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I pursue arts. I also pursue literature. A foreigner cannot have such an accent, so I thought that he was also a person with the similar heritage as I had. I recognised a certain, kind of, humanitarian attitude. I used to help the Jews from Russia and placed them in different jobs in Austria. So I thought that he was an Austrian too. There was a German minority in Yugoslavia called Volksdeutscher, and I asked him whether he belonged to that minority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you met him, did you continue to see and associate with Mr. Delalic? In other words, in conversation with Mr. Delalic and other activists of the BH association, did you all discuss your potential involvement in this club?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: As we started talking, they recognised me as a football referee, and then they said, "We would like to establish a sports association which would involve football, volleyball, handball, basketball. Would you want to get involved in this?" At first, I declined it, but Ms. Zutka Delalic, and Mr. Dzemal Delalic, this was a bit later, and Zejnil Delalic too, they said, "You know the methodology, and you know the education. You have education skills and you have a Slavic background. Would you set up and conduct language courses?" I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you conduct these courses?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: About two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you trying to help all the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of their ethnic background, or were these lectures geared only to the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I wouldn't have agreed to that. My students were Bosniaks, Serbs, Croats from Bosnia, Serbs from Serbia, the workers who work in the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Tomann, that this association organised a number of humanitarian activities to assist their population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and do you know whether Zejnil Delalic also took an active part through contributions, through suggestions, and in other ways?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. Starting with that exhibition, and I saw that there were people from all over the former Yugoslavia. There was even Mr. Bogdanovic, the mayor of the city of Belgrade, who later came back to this club and held lectures. He is well-known. He built a number of wartime memorials. Unfortunately, I have to say, a number of these monuments and now been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Tomann, was whether Zejnil Delalic also took an active part in all these humanitarian activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Of course, yes, yes. We had an executive board which met, and we had ideas and we made agreements. However, Mr. Delalic lived in Munich at the time, and we would invite him, and he would come and he would take part, mostly as a sponsor, donor, and in organisational matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a person who knows Mr. Zejnil Delalic, is he a humane person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Yes. That is my conviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From reports that you received as a member of the association, could you see that he frequently was one of the instigators of these humanitarian activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I will mention just a few. It was one that concerned the sick and the wounded. Then it was one for the electric power, utilities, then for schools. My group was in charge of a collection of medicine and clothing. All this was sent, and all this was posted. It was all recorded who did what. Mr. Delalic gave the largest individual financial contribution. We led the whole thing, but he was one of us. He was not a leader of it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did Zejnil Delalic, at any point, either during the collection of humanitarian aid or in organising any of the events showed any kind of hostility towards the Serbian population, or did he ever, for instance, insist that the aid should be sent just to the Muslims, or was his attitude the opposite of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, madam. Everybody used to come to this club, and this is what this club will continue to do. There are Bosniaks who have been in the west longer than Mr. Delalic who only pursued their own interests, and they sent their aid just to one side, but our aid went to everyone, regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomann, this cosmopolitan approach of Mr. Delalic, was it something that was expressed also through his sports activities where all Bosnian citizens who were refugees in Austria were gathering around?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I am very proud, because I am a member of this club, because this is the policy. At first, Mr. Delalic was the president of this sports association in Austria, but as he lived in Germany and as the association grew, as more people kept coming, he couldn't continue in that position any longer, so he stepped down and he was given an honour position, a position of an honorary head. In our club, we are multi-national. We have over 400 members. Out of them, 50 are of Serbian ethnic background. There are some Macedonians who were driven out of the Yugoslav league in Austria, so they play with us. In Austria, there is a Yugoslav league and a Croatian league, but in those leagues, in those associations, no person of another ethnic background ever plays.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tomann, can you tell me in brief, throughout this period of your association with Mr. Delalic through different activities in 1994 and 1995, what are your views of Mr. Delalic as a person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: I have many things in common with Mr. Delalic. He's younger than I am, but we have the same kind of upbringing. My mother gave me examples, moral examples from Talmud, from the Koran, and from the Bible. She told me to go to different neighbours and associate with different people, so it was an honour for us when the Muslims would invite us to their religious holidays, and we would invite them back to our holidays. Another thing that I have in common with Mr. Delalic is that he is well-versed in humanities, in philosophy and literature. One of his favourite writers is Isaac Bashivas-Singer, who is one of my own favourite writers, also Hume, Carl Pauper, are his favourite philosophers, just as they are mine. I saw him as a person of high education.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomann, do you think that Mr. Delalic could harm anyone, the person that you met?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: No. I am convinced that he could not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomann, the way you saw Mr. Delalic, was he a person that could see somebody in trouble and suffering and not help him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: From what I know about him, I don't think that he could even hurt a fly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomann, knowing Mr. Zejnil Delalic as you do, could you say whether Mr. Delalic could ever agree, if he would agree with anyone who would harm others?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: There were attempts, there were attempts to break up our association, and unfortunately, it came from Bosnia and Herzegovina. These attempts were made, but we did not allow that. Mr. Zejnil Delalic was one of the first, he and I both, and this whole leadership did not allow this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Tomann, is it true that, upon your arrival in The Hague, you gave me a catalogue of this art exhibition where you first met Mr. Delalic and where Mr. Delalic's words have been printed, as were Mr. Simon Wiesenthal's. Did you give me this catalogue as corroboration of your presence there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO TOMANN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I think I forgot. Yes, I turned this over to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have made a translation of the address of Mr. Wiesenthal and of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, and these words speak of Mr. Delalic's character. We have included it in our motion, and the witness confirmed that he personally submitted it to us and that he participated in this. I, here, have the original of this catalogue, and I tender it as an exhibit in evidence. Could you please hand it over to Their Honours, even though this has been enclosed within our motion. This concludes my questioning of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D204/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this admitted into evidence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me look at it, if there is any need for it. Let me see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have already requested translation into English. We are now submitting the original, which was provided to us by this witness. Inside, you will find the words addressed by Mr. Delalic in 1994. The original text contains the words of Mr. Delalic on the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which of them are you putting in? Here, the one I see, "Always together," I think that is the one you have in mind, February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the whole document. We have translated the words, that is the speech of Mr. Wiesenthal, Mr. Orban, various artists from different ethnic backgrounds who exhibited during the show, as well as the words of Mr. Zejnil Delalic who was one of the organisers of the show which clearly show what kind of man he was, what kind of cosmopolitan he was, even after he left the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose it's associated with the publications, and this is what you want to show, that he is associated with what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You might well put it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any examination of him? Any examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you are discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence calls Witness Darko Ruzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you please introduce yourself to the Court by stating your full name?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: My name is Darko Ruzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruzic, what is your ethnic background and what is your nationality, citizenship?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat by nationality and I'm a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your profession, Mr. Ruzic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: I completed technical college, and before that, I completed vocational school and was trained as a locksmith.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you first meet Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: The first time I met Mr. Delalic was at the beginning of August on the Igman platform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruzic, was that at the time when Mr. Zejnil Delalic took over the duty of the commander of the Tactical Group and came to Igman?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was at the beginning of the action whose objective was to lift the siege of Sarajevo. It was the operation called JUG '92.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you do before the war? Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: For about 20 years, I worked at the technical institute which worked for the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of job were you supposed to get at the beginning of August when you saw Mr. Delalic on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: I spent as an analyst of technical materials, I spent some time working on that issue for about five years. So I was involved with weapons, and I worked in Zadar, Kalinovik, and other places in the former Yugoslavia. I also worked as an inspector of weapons for the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Territorial Defence, and did you go to Mount Igman in that capacity, that is, to take over a certain amount of artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Territorial Defence before the aggression on Hadzici. I was also a member of the Patriotic League. At the beginning of the aggression, I went to the area of Pazaric which, at that time, was the free territory in that area. At the beginning, I worked with certain municipality bodies, and I was also involved in preparations of the JUG '92 operation. I was supposed to take over a certain amount of artillery weapons, that is, T-55, T-133 millimetre gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that capacity, you were deployed on the main axis of the JUG '92 operation. The Court knows quite a few things about that. I'm not going to go into any details, but I would like to know whether you provided support to Zejnil Delalic at one point, who was the commander of the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the commander of a battery, and I had certain assignments in that respect. I know that Mr. Zejnil Delalic was the commander of the Tactical Group 1 in the place called Ormanj. Whenever the Serbian artillery would open fire from Rakovica and the neighbouring areas, we would use our gun, the so-called Sultan, and we would often receive requests to provide support and to return fire to the Serbian artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, but I'm not interested in combat activities. We've been listening about that for 18 months now. My question to you, Mr. Ruzic, is whether you had an opportunity to meet, to get to know Zejnil Delalic as a person throughout that period of time?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruzic, what was Delalic's personal attitude toward his fighters, to other combatants.

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: I had a very positive impression of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, and it was an honour for me that Zejnil Delalic, together with another friend of ours, who had been a member of the JNA, to become members -- who became a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it was an honour for me that Zejnil Delalic wanted to spend some time on Bjelasnica with us, together with a number of my superior officers and my soldiers. He wanted to spend a few hours with us, and we gladly shared the little food we had with him. So we would sort of take some time off together whenever it was possible to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had quite a few informal encounters with Mr. Delalic, in spite of the intensive fighting that was going on at the time. Did you notice Mr. Delalic, did you observe any different attitude by Mr. Delalic in respect of you, who are a Croat?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, and even later in 1992, 1993, as a member of the BH army, first a member of the Territorial Defence, and then member of the BH army, I never experienced any nationalistic hatred. I never experienced that from Mr. Delalic, in particular, who always wanted to spend some time in friendly conversation with me and others. This was never an issue with us. Even if we did discuss these things, Mr. Delalic, as commander of the Tactical Group, as someone who had a superior position, insisted that we should adopt and behave in accordance with our strict moral principles in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Later on when you provided support to his units, did you ever observe any kind of hostility towards other people because they were of different ethnic or religious background?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: No, I never noticed that kind of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We all know that the war causes a lot of misfortune. What kind of attitude did Zejnil Delalic have towards his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Zejnil Delalic, as a commander of the Tactical Group 1 and who was a superior to me in the chain of command, always paid attention to his men, always took proper care of his men. He never allowed any wounded soldier to be left behind, and he never allowed us to behave differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The weapon that you were in charge of, the gun that you mentioned, is a large calibre gun, and it's quite destructive. When you provided support to Tactical Group 1, which was under the command of Zejnil Delalic, did he, did Zejnil Delalic ever tell you, ever warn you, as to the targets that should not be covered by that heavy weapon?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this was not something that we would discuss during a military operation. During a military operation, we knew exactly what our targets were. However, outside combat, outside battle, when we would discuss things in general, he would insist on that. He bore in mind the fact that we did not have enough weapons and ammunition, and he insisted on the fact that we should only limit ourselves to military targets. He was aware that this is something that we could bank on after the war, after the victory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruzic, the Court is aware of the fact how we were all hungry in 1992. However, do you know that occasionally in Pazaric, where Zejnil Delalic had his headquarters, do you know that members of Zejnil Delalic's family would go there, would come there from abroad, and bring you things which were so precious for you at the time, like, canned food, cigarettes, and so on. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We all knew about that. It wasn't only Zejnil Delalic, but there were also others who had well-off families abroad and who would send us equipment, cigarettes, food. I don't know the family of Zejnil Delalic personally, and I didn't know them at the time; however, it was common knowledge that Zejnil Delalic, Ziam Civic who were not stationed at Igman were the ones who provided food, cigarettes and other necessities through their families. We knew that whenever Zejnil would come, there would be more cigarettes and food for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could it happen that Zejnil Delalic got a large carton of cigarettes and keep them for himself?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: No. We would all have them. We would all share them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could Zejnil Delalic smoke a pack of cigarettes himself, or would he always share that one pack of cigarettes that he had at the time?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Whenever he had a pack of cigarettes, it would lie on the table. It was offered to everyone. He would share his last cigarette with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruzic, you were a member of the Territorial Defence and, later on, a soldier in the Bosnian army. Could you tell me, throughout the JUG '92 operation, that is, August, September, October, 1992, what was the ethnic composition of Zejnil Delalic's units? Was there a significant number of Bosnian Serbs that were members of his unit?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: As you could see from what I have said, there was no nationalistic hostility among us, and the composition of the Territorial Defence and, later on, the composition of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was mixed. I used to say that the Bosnian army very well represented the Bosnian country, Bosnia and Herzegovina in general. It's an ethnically mixed society. In my unit, I had people from various ethnic backgrounds, and when it comes to the JUG '92 operation, I can tell you that, for example, the Zenica Brigade supplied one battalion for the operation, and there were over 30 per cent of Serbs in that battalion, which is a higher percentage of Serbs. That does not reflect, for example, the actual situation in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned Cedo Domaz who lived in the same residential block in Zenica. Are you talking about a BH army soldier who was killed later on but was declared a national hero after his death?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cedo Domaz was a member of the Patriotic League, and he came to Igman one month before I did, and he became a legend. He was buried in Brezovaca, and he received the so-called Golden Fleur de Lys as this is the highest military decoration in the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a battalion in the Zenica Brigade which has 30 per cent Serbs in it. Was this a similar situation in the unit under the command of Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the precise hierarchy, but in Ormanj, in the area of Ormanj, I know, because I was involved with providing logistics support in that area, I know that they also had the village of Tvrdimici under their responsibility, and I provided support to them as well. The battalion that first completed the task and stopped in the village of Tvrdimici, one day before we managed to arrive in Stojcevac, I know that was the case with that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zejnil Delalic had the same kind of attitude towards all soldiers, and did he retain that kind of attitude throughout your acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: I never had any doubts as to the behaviour and attitude of Mr. Zejnil Delalic towards me and towards other people he came in contact with. I simply cannot accept the possibility that Zejnil Delalic would behave differently somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To conclude, Mr. Ruzic, if you can just briefly tell me, what was your view, what was your idea, of Zejnil Delalic as a man? What can you say about him as a man?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Well, since you ask me that question, I have to add a few things. When I joined the Territorial Defence and the BH army, and the first persons, in general, who joined the Territorial Defence and the BH army, they were the real Bosniaks like myself. They were the people who wanted to prevent the aggression, to prevent the war. Zejnil Delalic was one of the persons who joined the Territorial Defence first, together with other worthy Bosniaks. They were the real Bosniaks. They were the real fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Zejnil Delalic, from the beginning of August until the end of autumn, did he remain the same? Did he remain humane? Did he remain a true Bosniak, which, in our parts, implies religious and national tolerance? Did he ever change?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that, not only in that period, but still today, these people, these fighters think of Zejnil Delalic as a good person and as a true Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about Zejnil Delalic from the period prior to August 1992. You don't know anything about how he lived before, and you don't know what happened to him after he left Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That concludes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No questions for Mr. Mucic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Ruzic, did you ever work for Mr. Delalic in and about the city of Konjic, or was it only up on Mount Igman that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: I met him only at the beginning of August on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was the only place where you were in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the only place, because I spent a lot of time on Mount Igman. I would stay there for two or three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason why you weren't a member of the HVO as opposed to the TO, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: I was never a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was wondering if there was any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: If you followed me closely, you could have noticed that I said at the beginning, I said that all Bosnians behaved the same. I lived in the area of Hadzici. I wanted to be as close to home as possible, and I was expelled from my home by Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you ever recall, during the time that you knew him, Mr. Delalic being referred to by a code name or a military name?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of his attitude to people of different ethnic groups. Did you ever observe or hear him express his attitude towards the enemy when you were engaged in military activities?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, no, never, except when we would discuss things freely at my unit, and the code of conduct of soldiers towards their enemy. We didn't have any other conversations of that kind. No, I never felt any attitude towards the enemy expressed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him refer to the enemy by names such as "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about prisoners of war, were you ever able to hear him express his attitude about prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: No. As I told you, Mr. Zejnil Delalic would only come during his free time, and his attitudes towards prisoners of war, if he was the same, but I don't know whether he had any contacts with prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you consider Mr. Delalic to be an honest man?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think that he would ever state untrue things or exaggerate in order to protect himself?

utterances.speaker: DARKO RUZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you are discharged now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good time for a break. Do you want me to call my witness after the break? This is the last witness for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will break now and reassemble at noon. So you will call your witness then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I call our last witness, I promised you that I would provide you with a copy of a translation of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My office was able to provide it, so I would like to submit it to you. This is the integral text of the Criminal Code, which Professor Tomic used when he testified. I have provided copies for each one of Your Honours and for the Prosecutor as well. If I can ask the usher's assistance to distribute the copies. Also, my office in Sarajevo was able to find the text of the Yugoslav Criminal Code, and we are working on copying that, and I will provide that to you. In this way, you will have all the pertinent documents that were discussed through the witness Professor Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is not necessary to have these exhibits marked, and my apologies for interrupting you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. We can have them as they are. Kindly bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The next witness is Almina Cilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam. Would you please introduce yourself to the Court by stating your full name?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Almina Cilic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us where you were born and what is your ethnic background and your citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: I was born on 22 May, 1959 in Ostrozac in the Jablanica municipality. I am a Bosniak by ethnic background, and I'm a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: I'm a graduate of law school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Cilic, are you related to Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zejnil Delalic is my uncle. He is the brother of my deceased father, Dzafer Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where does your family come from?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: From Ostrozac in the Jablanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Ostrozac, where both you and Mr. Delalic were born, do people of different ethnic backgrounds also live there, that is, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. The people of all ethnic backgrounds, there were a lot of Serbs, and maybe just four Croatian families, but our population was mixed, and we all live well together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the economic status of the Delalic family?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic or, I should say, my Uncle Zejnil was born in a very poor family with nine children, seven brothers and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the children from this family go to school, and did Zejnil Delalic go to school, specifically?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. All children went to school. The two girls completed elementary school, and the boys finished some secondary school, and Zejnil completed high school and then college in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Ms. Cilic, what your uncle did after he graduated?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, after he graduated, he first was employed in the labour bureau in Sarajevo, and after that, he went to Germany and started his own successful business.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you said, he came from a very poor family. You probably are not aware of his early childhood or youth. You're much younger. After your uncle became a successful businessman, did he forget his parents?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. He took great care of his parents. He frequently visited them, not only during his vacations, but at certain holidays. He always made sure that they had medical assistance if they were sick, and he also supported them financially so that they did not lack anything. They had everything, and he made sure that they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Uncle Zejnil did not forget about his parents. What about his relationship with his brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: I know that he supported his brothers and sisters. For instance, if they had a problem with housing, he would contribute money to help finish the house or buy an apartment. If they wanted to start a business, they knew that they could rely on him, and often times, they didn't need to specifically go to him and ask him. He would find out and he would help them on his own. So he really supported them consistently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your aunts, Sefkija and Hajena, Zejnil's sisters, both were widowed early. What was Zejnil's relation to them and their children?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: I think that he had a special relation to them, because he was aware that they were widowed very young. And also, the lost of a father is irreplaceable, but he tried to, at least, make sure that they did not have any financial problems, and, indeed, he really helped them a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Zejnil struggled to put himself through school. Did he take care that his siblings' children also received a good education?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a few children in our family, and almost all of us have gone through school, and I wanted to study, and he was very glad to hear that I wanted to do so. He immediately asked if he could help us financially, and my father did not have much money, so an arrangement was made. I studied law, and my brothers studied mechanical engineering, and he would give us 200 German marks monthly throughout this time. I have actually kept receipts from banks as a kind of souvenir.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This money which you kept receiving, and your brother and maybe some other members of your family too, over a period of four years, was this money the only help that your uncle sent you in order to help you get an education?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: It was not the only help. He would also, whenever he would come home, bring presents, different kinds of presents. He took both myself and my brother to Germany so that we would meet different people, so that we would meet his friends. There were a lot of people that we met, including Germans, so that we would learn the language a little bit, so that we could expand our horizons and learn another culture. So he made it possible for us to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the evidence that has been presented to the Court so far, the Court knows that two of his brothers died on the same day, and there were some under-aged children who were left fatherless. How did Zejnil treat those children?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: In 1993, in a single day, two of my uncles died, Sefik and Vesil, Sefik in Vienna, and Vesil in Zagreb. One of them left behind a daughter, and Vesil had two sons, and Zejnil provided all assistance that he could so that the family would not be wanting because of the loss of a father. So he helped them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say that all of you in the family who lost a parent, Zejnil helped to the extent that he could in order for you not to feel the loss too much?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because another uncle of mine, Rasim, also died, and he helped his daughter as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does Zejnil Delalic have his own children?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zejnil has a son and a daughter. The son just graduated. We saw each other recently. He graduated from the secondary medical school, and he is now going to go on with his education. His daughter Sandra is also putting herself through school studying commerce.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask you: Who is Zejnil Delalic's wife?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Her name is Gordana and she was born in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is her ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: She is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When Zejnil Delalic married a Serbian woman from Belgrade who came to live in Konjic, how did the Delalic family receive Gordana?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Fine. There was no problem that she was Serbian. Even though Zejnil's mother was a religious person, she did not mind that she was of another religious background, and she accepted her as her own daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please say, as a member of the family, who was supporting Zejnil Delalic's children who lived with their mother in Belgrade until Zejnil was brought here and detained?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: It was Zejnil who supported them. He provided for their living expenses, and they frequently visited him during school vacations. He bought them a wonderful house in Belgrade, and he supported them financially, anything they needed. I know about this because I talked about it with Mrs. Gordana. I saw her recently. We talked about everything, including this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Gordana Delalic, wife of Zejnil Delalic, had a serious traffic accident and she is unable to work. Who supported her before Zejnil was arrested?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. She had a very serious traffic accident, and she is still recovering from the consequences of that. Right now, we are able to provide enough money to Gordana and the children in Belgrade so that they do not lack of what they need. They are used to living rather well, and we are trying to help them, and we will continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Cilic, even though Mr. Delalic's wife and children live in Belgrade, have you ever heard Zejnil Delalic speak badly about his wife, and did they continue to maintain a decent relationship throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: I have been with them a lot of times, but he's a gentleman. I've never heard him say anything bad. He always treated me in a gentlemanly manner, and he also treated his wife in the same way. I think that they continue to maintain relations. She has visited him a number of times here. Now, I don't know all the details about their private relations, but from everything I know, from all the conversations I've had, I think that she wouldn't be doing this had he treated her badly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that she has visited him a number of times, along with the children?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that they came a number of times here in The Hague, both she and the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Zejnil Delalic is a person who helped his immediate family and also helped his wider family. Do you know, regarding this humane approach of his, did he also help other people?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. He helped quite a number of people down there. He helped some financially. He helped somebody find a job. He helped somebody open a private business. He also supported cultural events, as well as sports activities. He also contributed to schools in providing teaching aids, equipment, and such.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Konjic municipality, which is where the Delalic family comes from, was not a very rich community, but people engaged in different types of activities. Do you know whether your uncle helped develop certain activities in your municipality before the war?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: I know that he specifically helped quite a bit in Ostrozac. He was one of the founders of the sports association and club, water sports association, in particular. It was windsurfing equipment and kayaks, and I don't know what else this equipment is. He organised some regattas. It was a small community, and without his financial support, I don't think they would have been able to organise all these activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that you were not in Jablanica in 1992, but I know that you came back there later, even though there were terrible rumours. People were saying that he was a member of the Serbian Secret Service and things like that. Do you know something about his life after he left Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Even after he left, I know that he supported people. I know that my mother went to Germany in 1994, and he sent 10.000 German marks to help provide flour in Ostrozac and distribute it among the population. There were Serbs living there, and even a few Croats, and this was distributed evenly to everyone in Ostrozac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zejnil was married to a Serbian woman from Serbia, and there were other mixed marriages in your family. How did your family view members of different ethnic groups once they became members of your family?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are other mixed marriages in my family. My sister is married to a Serb and lives in Belgrade. Another cousin is married to a Croat. This is a normal thing, that people do not distinguish. What was important was whether somebody was a good person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the close family, do you know whether Zejnil Delalic ever engaged in politics?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was interested in business. He's, first of all, a businessperson. I'm not aware of him engaging in politics, at least he hasn't to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, Ms. Cilic, you said that as an uncle, he also treated you as a gentleman. I want to ask you whether he showed respect to all people, or did he try to be above them?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: No. I think that if anything, he would, sort of, even take a step down so that people would feel comfortable. You know, we're all the same, and for him, every person was a worthwhile person. This is how he treated everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Cilic, did your uncle show feelings towards people?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. Even though he is trying to hide it a little bit, I know that he's a very sensitive person, and I notice that very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever put down other people?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: No. I never noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In so far as you know Mr. Delalic, could he harm anyone?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: No. He's not such a person. He always sought to help people. It is a bit unusual for a person to help people so much, but I felt that he took pleasure from helping others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say that he, himself, could not harm anyone, but in so far as you know your uncle, do you think that your uncle would accept or agree if somebody else was doing harm to someone else?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: I think that he would try to prevent it. I know that if he was aware of it that he would try to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Cilic, if someone were to ask you to give a brief comment on your uncle, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: As a person with a strong character, a humane person, a gentleman, a very highly educated person. I also graduated from college, but I never knew as much as he did about various areas of knowledge. Again, as I said, also he is somebody who helps people, and I really don't know anything negative that I could say about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Cilic, you are a member of the family, and this is your perception of your uncle, but you also move among other people. Have you ever noticed that any of the people that you have come in touch with who knew your uncle said anything bad about him?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: There may be people who have something against him, but all the people that I'm aware of perceive him as I do. This is a small community, and most people know him there, and they perceive him as a humanitarian. Perhaps there are people who believe in some kind of propaganda or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Finally, Zejnil Delalic was arrested in March of 1996. At that time, you were in Jablanica. Can you tell me what the reaction was when this news came?

utterances.speaker: ALMINA CILIC
utterances.text: The citizens of Jablanica were very surprised. A number of them came to me and said, "How can we help? He did not deserve it." We actually expected that he would be awarded for what he had done, rather than get arrested. Nobody still knows why this has happened. Really, people wanted to help. It was difficult for them, and they still, to date, approach me and ask me how he is, how he is enduring all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My last question to you, Ms. Cilic: In fact, you already said that your uncle was sending you money for four years. This is your foreign currency account which you have provided me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have tendered a copy of this, and I'm not going to tender the original booklet here. This concludes my examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any examination of this witness by any other counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No questions on behalf of Mr. Mucic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This concludes your witnesses for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have come to the end of our witness list, that is, character witnesses, that we want to call for the purpose of the sentencing hearing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are discharged now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court has given us permission to supplement with Mrs. Delic's statement. We have a sick copying machine so all we have is one copy. The Prosecutor has seen it and, I believe, has no objection, and the Registry has agreed to copy it and distribute it to the members of the Tribunal. We would move to introduce this as the next Delic number. Secondly, we have previously provided the Trial Chamber with copies of the English translation of two statements. We have the original Bosnian, if the Court would like them. If the Court doesn't want them, whatever pleases the Court. One is from Mr. Delic's father, and the other is from Salem Delic. Again, you already have the English translations. Whatever pleases the Court pleases me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As long as you've submitted them, I think it's sufficient for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Instead of cluttering the file with more paper, we will just leave these. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: If Mr. Moran is finished, there's a matter that I need to bring up before the Court, if this is an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: The Defence of Esad Landzo filed a motion for acceptance of additional written statements as evidence relevant to sentencing of Esad Landzo. It was in my box this morning, but after talking to my friend and colleague, Tom Moran, he had not seen it as of shortly before -- as of an hour or so ago. I also showed the motion to Teresa McHenry and to Grant Niemann, and my understanding is they had not seen it either. So I guess my first question is was this in your boxes this morning? Have you had an opportunity to see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. We've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Certainly, Tom has already told me that he plans to object, but I would just like to ask the Court that this be accepted into evidence based on two Rules, Rule 84(A)(vi), presentation of evidence, which states: "Any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence, if the accused is found guilty on one or more charges in the indictment." The second relevant Rule is Rule 100, pre-sentencing procedure, which states: "If the accused pleads guilty or if the Trial Chamber finds the accused guilty of a crime, the Prosecutor and the Defence may submit any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence." Clearly, the important words in both of those Rules are "any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence." As you can see from the motion, Mr. Jelisic does not want to come back to court and testify again to clear up the false impression that his last statement clearly left. I understand that an article was published yesterday in a Serb newspaper criticising him for coming to court and testifying for a Muslim, testifying for Esad Landzo. I would ask that since the Court has shown flexibility all week long in admitting written statements, even Mr. Delic's Defence finished Tuesday and just offered a written statement which, of course, he did have your permission, and I think Mr. Mucic's Defence also mentioned that they were going to be turning in some things, we would ask that the Court accept our motion as well and enter that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any objection on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just received it a few minutes ago. We're deferring to the Court as to whether or not you believe it would be helpful or appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just toss a few thoughts out here. This man took the witness stand and essentially shut down a cross-examination by refusing to answer questions. Now to come back without the ability for me or anyone else to cross-examine him, it's a highly unusual procedure, to say the least. I've never heard of such a thing. If this man wants to answer questions, fine, then he can take the witness stand and answer questions. If the Court decides or someone else thinks that it's necessary to have some protection for him, this Court is well familiar with protecting witnesses from threats and other things. But to testify and then refuse to be subjected to cross-examination, and then to submit a written statement that's uncross-examinable, to me, is something I've never heard of before, either in a guilt or a sentencing proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: If I might just respond. It's also a highly unusual procedure for a situation like we had yesterday or the day before, where Mr. Delic spoke directly to Esad Landzo. We objected. The Court accepted that testimony, allowed that to happen, has been very flexible all week long. I would simply ask, in light of the fact that there's no objection from the Prosecution and they are deferring to the Court, I would just ask that the Court allow that to be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It will be admitted. Actually, what weight do you attach to it yourself as counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I believe you asked me what weight I attached to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. What weight do you attach to that type of testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Well, my understanding is that the Court will attach whatever weight -- as the trier of fact, you will attach whatever weight you choose to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I would just ask that we be given the opportunity to, at least, present it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To say what he refused to say when he was in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just tell you that I was caught by surprise, as I think everybody was. He did go home that night, back to the detention centre, and wrote a statement which he gave to us the next day. We had it translated the next day and filed it as part of the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All that the witness said, the gist of what he said, is he is a very nice man. He entertains. He has no prejudices. That's all. That's what you wanted him to say. He said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How does this statement help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No. What he now wants to say is the question which arose when he refused to lead his immunity. He wants that in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Right. I do want that in. Clearly, that's mitigation, and I ask that the Court accept it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why did he refuse to say it under oath?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: My understanding was -- well, as I state it in the motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's not fair. That's not fair, because if he refused to say it when he was before the Trial Chamber, it would be unusual for him to go away and then say it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I agree with you that in this case there have been lots of unusual things that have happened in this case. I can see that you're leaning toward not allowing me to admit that into evidence, and I will ask that, again, since there's no objection from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How does it further support his statement? I've told you what the gist of his statement is, and what he's said doesn't hurt Mr. Moran's client. Why should he be objecting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You're asking me, Your Honour? Your Honour, the question was, "Were you told by Mr. Landzo that he was going to get on the witness stand and lie," and when he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see the question of guilt and innocence is not to be decided on the basis of these statements. The statements will be taken into account only when the question of the quantum of sentence is being considered. If somebody wants to produce evidence to say that he is a very nice man, that he has no prejudices, that he is feeling very sorry, and it's probably the leaders who got them into all of this is, the point which you cited --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will be one thing that I will discuss in my final submissions, and I'm going to ask you not to consider involving my client with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But it doesn't involve your client. The evidence with regard to sentencing is very individual in the sense that everyone speaks for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and my client spoke for himself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have some doubts whether one witness can be cross-examined by the other. It's very personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the procedures that I'm used to when there are multiple defendants, if it comes time for sentencing, the Court brings in the first defendant and does what the Court's going to do, and then brings in the next defendant. It's a totally separate procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is the usual course. In the situation of a joint trial, it doesn't come in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You're right. I've never been involved in any proceeding quite like this sentencing proceeding because of four defendants at the same time, but the Court has handled it as well as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Rule, as it is framed by us, does envisage some sort of cross-examination by the other counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
