utterances.text: Otherwise, it's a personal effort of every accused to show that he should not be given a more severe sentence than would normally be awarded in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I concur with you completely. It's a time to bring in mitigating evidence and aggravating evidence, where the Prosecution wishes to show that someone is a bad person, or I wish to show that someone's a good person. It's the time to do that. It's also a time for the Court to get to know defendants as people. You've seen four people sitting here, four bodies, but this is a chance for you to know who they are. I think that is one of the more important things that this proceeding has done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In the interests of the credibility of your witness, I don't think you need to pursue that motion. It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say in the interests of the credibility of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You do not need to pursue that motion, because it's not coming in to be of any assistance to what he has said before in other respects.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I will ask that, even though that may be true, based on what his testimony involved, clearly, his hesitance to answer a question that, based on the motion, you will see that he believed that that was -- I've forgotten the word now that we used, but he did not want any adverse reaction from any of the other defendants. When he came here, that was not his intent, to be critical of any of the other defendants, but I believe that left a false impression, and I would like to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When considering the charges against your client, the Defence of your client was that he committed some of these crimes under the influence of Delic. When we consider that, whether that statement can be relied upon or not when considering his guilt, then that finding may have some bearing on the question of sentence if he was acting under influence. But this statement which he made, this witness has nothing to do with it, but he wants now to further explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: So you don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Basically his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's of no assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- was that your client is a very fine gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Because you were both speaking at the same time, I just didn't hear the first part of your sentence, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His evidence was that your client is a very fine gentleman. He entertains. He looks after things, socialises, has no prejudices.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: The gist was also just to show that they achieve some harmony in the prison between the ethnic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How does this statement really help his explanation?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Again, rather than so much helping the things that you've just spoken to, in my view, it leaves a false impression that weighs heavily on my client's credibility. He is the only defendant who took the stand and testified for two days, and I would just hate for that one instance to profoundly affect the way the Trial Chamber view his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We've looked at the sequence and the way this statement is now being suggested to be admitted. It was denied. It was refused, him claiming immunity. Then when he left, he thought it over again, and now he wants it to come in without cross-examination. He wants it to be admitted without cross-examination, in which case it has no effect on whatever he must have said and, thereby, raises doubts on the question which was put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it sounds like you've listened to everything that I can say. If it's not to be admitted into evidence, if that's your decision, then that's your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm saying that even if it was there, it's counterproductive and cannot be of any use to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: At the risk of asking the same thing over and over and over, I will now sit down. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, when are you starting your address?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, we're ready to start, Your Honour, but considering it's five minutes to one -- in fact, my colleague Ms. McHenry will start, and then I will follow after her presentation. We're ready to commence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All right. Utilise the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I make application that we put it over. It's difficult to interrupt it and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Because in any event -- you mean you want a full one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. As I said yesterday, it will take longer than an hour. I said when we made our original submissions to Your Honours, we said that we wanted half a day last Monday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For summarising what has happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. We've never had an opportunity to address the Defence's submissions, and we need to do that, to make our oral submissions as a consequence of the submissions they've made. We've never had that opportunity. They had that opportunity because they received ours first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In spite of your submissions, you still have extensive submissions to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is no way, in our submissions, could we anticipate what they put in their submissions which we received after we had filed ours. Their submissions were written with the benefit of having our submissions available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It might be understanding the philosophy of punishment and sentencing, which is one thing, but it doesn't have to be as extensive as that. Whatever aggravation or whatever mitigation you have might have been out of the proceedings we've already heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've sat here all week without having any submissions at all, and we haven't responded to their submissions. I mean, surely the Prosecution is going to be given an opportunity to respond to their written submissions. We could have done it in writing, if Your Honours had so ordered, but we understood it to be done by way of oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may well start.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did I understand, Your Honour, that you would like me to start now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like you to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I know you know what you're doing, but I'm just saying it, please don't touch on the merits of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We did not intend to touch on the merits of the case. I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Still, I thought I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, we're also not intending to repeat what was said in our written submission. What we would like to do is just emphasise a couple of points and, in particular, to respond to certain points made by the Defence in their written submission and then throughout this week in their oral presentations. I will speak about the two accused who made their presentations first, Mr. Landzo and Mr. Delic, and then Mr. Niemann will speak about Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delalic. I would note that systems differ as to whether the Prosecution is expected to give a recommendation to the Judges about its view of the proper sentence for a particular accused. In some systems, it is not considered appropriate to do so, while in other systems, it is customary to do so and, indeed, it would be considered inappropriate not to give a recommendation. For a variety of different reasons, the Prosecutor Justice Arbour has adopted the policy of giving a sentence recommendation and, thus, in every case before this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal, the Prosecution has given its recommendation. Consistent with this policy, it would be our intention to give Your Honours our view as to a recommended sentence, unless we are directed to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: -- unless we are directed not to do so by Your Honours. Obviously, the Defence has presented material and evidence from families and friends of the accused to the effect that the witness considers each of the accused to be a nice person. Indeed, it would be rare for an accused not to have family members or friends who think that and probably in every case before this Tribunal, there would be some evidence. The Prosecution does not, in fact, contest that the accused have persons would care for them and have seen them to be nice persons. However, these and similar other facts raised in this case, although relevant, are of limited weight. For not only are these facts not unusual, more importantly in this case, they are not ones that would entitle the accused to a significantly lower sentence. The most important facts, as pointed out in our brief with citations, and I believe that Judge Karibi-Whyte has alluded to this several times, the most important considerations for sentencing are those that are already presented during the trial. They are the factors that relate to the crimes for which the accused will have been convicted, including the gravity of the offence and the accused's role in these crimes. Your Honours have heard about the gravity of the offences, and you have heard for how, over seven months, persons were imprisoned in Celebici, many of whom, most of whom, should never have been imprisoned at all, much less for months on end, and how they were treated. I won't repeat the evidence. I can't even repeat all of it. I would just ask, when finally deciding on a sentence, that you think about and remember the hundreds of victims of the Celebici camp, that you think about what their lives were like, how a large number of them did not survive, and how even those who did survive will be scarred, physically or emotionally or both, for the rest of their lives. As found by the Chamber in the Kambanda case in the Rwanda Tribunal, sentences should reflect the predominant standard of proportionality between the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender. As also noted in that decision, fair sentences contribute to the respect for the law and the maintenance of a just and peaceful society. This Tribunal is only concerned with serious violations of international humanitarian law. It is expected that the majority of sentences here, as opposed to national systems which deal predominantly with less severe crimes, will be severe. Indeed, in cases with significant loss of life, it should not be surprising if the majority of the sentences imposed by this Tribunal are the most severe possible. In this case, the Celebici case, the gravity of the offences committed by the accused and the degree of responsibility attended to each defendant are high. The crimes carry an intrinsic gravity, and their atrocious, cruel, and repetitive nature is shocking to the human conscience. Given this, unduly light sentences would be contrary to justice and the fundamental purpose of this Tribunal. As I said, we're going to go through the accused individually, and I'll start with Mr. Landzo. Mr. Landzo was a guard in the camp for a number of months. Mr. Landzo acted as a cruel and sadistic guard who took every opportunity to use his power to horribly mistreat the detainees. Sometimes he did it because he was ordered to do so, and sometimes he did it on his own initiative. Mr. Landzo has made a number of different arguments in favour of mitigation and ultimately requested a five-year sentence. With all due respect to Mr. Landzo and his counsel, the Prosecution must begin its submission by stating that the recommendation of five years and, indeed, many of the arguments made by the Landzo Defence are, in our submission, ludicrous. Normally, we don't like to use such characterisations, but in this case, we feel it is necessary. I will address the points raised by the Landzo Defence in, more or less, the same order that they were raised in their written submission. The Defence first suggested that the accused Landzo, and I believe Mr. Delic has made a similar suggestion, turned themselves in. This is not a full and accurate characterisation of what happened, as the records of this Tribunal demonstrate. Mr. Landzo and Mr. Delic were indicted by this Tribunal. The indictment was public, and the indictments received a reasonable amount of publicity, including in Konjic where the accused were located. The accused did not turn themselves in to any international authority. Rather, the accused, Mr. Landzo, at least, gave interviews to the press talking about the indictment and the fact he knew about it, but they did not turn themselves in. Initially, there were no steps taken to arrest them by the Bosnian authorities, and after some weeks, I believe over a month, when the accused had neither turned themselves in, nor been arrested, the Prosecutor personally intervened at the highest levels, and the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina initiated action. We don't know how exactly the Bosnian authorities got custody of the accused and, thus, we are not in a position to contest any representations that they were directed by their local authorities to report to the police and that they did so. We can state categorically, however, that the accused, both Mr. Landzo and Mr. Delic, fought then their surrender to The Hague. Indeed, it was only after some time, after their challenges to their extradition or surrender were ultimately rejected by the Bosnian Supreme Court, that the accused were forcibly surrendered to this Tribunal. When the accused, Mr. Landzo and Mr. Delic, report that they spent 43 days in gaol in Sarajevo, that's not because the Tribunal or international authorities were slow in transporting them. It's because the accused challenged their extradition, and it took some time to work its way through the courts. In circumstances where an accused has fought his surrender to the Tribunal, we believe that there can be no legitimate claim that an accused deserves some sort of credit for turning himself in. We would note that the facts, including that there were challenges by the accused to their extradition, are noted in a number of court documents from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some of those ones which specifically reference the objections made by the accused are part of this Tribunal's record. If there's any question, we would refer Your Honours to the registry record for this case, including documents 337, 1337 bis, and 2337 bis. There are other documents, but I believe those state it. The accused, Mr. Landzo, then argues that he should get some kind of credit for an admission of guilt, in attempts to compare this case with that of Mr. Erdemovic, before this Tribunal. We believe there can be no comparison. In the Erdemovic case, the accused had not been indicted by this Tribunal. Indeed, the accused was not under investigation, and the Prosecution was not even aware of the specific incidents in which Mr. Erdemovic was involved. Mr. Erdemovic informed the Prosecution about the crimes he had been involved in. He cooperated fully, including giving truthful statements from the beginning, and he pled guilty immediately. There was no trial, saving a tremendous amount of expenditure of resources and not putting witnesses through the traumatic experience of testifying at trial. Of course, that is not the case here. Here, we are here almost two and a half years after Mr. Landzo was indicted, after a lengthy trial of almost one and a half years, which entailed significant expenditure of resources and significant trauma to the witnesses. Mr. Landzo still has never pled guilty to anything. The Prosecution fails to see how he can claim credit for admitting guilt when, in fact, he has not admitted his guilt. Indeed, you saw even this week, when the Prosecution referred to crimes committed by Mr. Landzo, the Defence objected and said that we were required to use the term "alleged crimes." The Defence then claims that Mr. Landzo acted under superior orders, and the Prosecution does agree that the evidence established that sometimes Mr. Landzo was acting under orders. We emphasise that in speaking of the evidence, we are including the evidence of the victims, who saw and heard when Mr. Landzo and other guards were sometimes ordered to mistreat victims. We are not relying solely on any uncorroberated testimony of Mr. Landzo. We believe that sometimes he was acting under orders, and this can sometimes be a relevant factor. The Prosecution believes, though, that under the circumstances of this case, this factor does not warrant a significantly reduced sentence, and we would note that there is no evidence of duress here. Indeed, the accused expressed no hesitation and, indeed, reported that he enjoyed carrying out his orders. Further, of course, on multiple occasions, Mr. Landzo acted out any superior orders whatsoever. The Defence next attempts to claim some sort of credit for an attempt to cooperate. We find this also unbelievable. We would first note that although the details are not important, the Prosecution, in its written submission, has accurately reported the one plea discussion that occurred between the Defence and the Prosecution. The events were independently remembered by both Mr. Niemann and myself, and they were the subject of a detailed memorandum to the file at the time. In any event, the main fact, and really the only important fact, is not in dispute, and that is that the accused approached the Prosecution about a potential plea, and there was no agreement for reasons including that the Prosecution was unwilling to contemplate recommending a sentence of five years because, in the view of the Prosecution, that would represent a travesty of justice. It's clear that the Defence did not approach the Prosecution just because the accused wanted to accept responsibility or as a sign of genuine remorse or to aid the truth-finding process or the attainment of justice. No. The accused made the strategic decision that it might be in Landzo's best interest to have a plea agreement if it was extremely, extremely generous. The Defence could not get the agreement they wanted, and they chose not to cooperate or plead guilty. We don't criticise Mr. Landzo for wanting to explore what was in his best interest, but the idea that by making an exploration, he's entitled to some sort of mitigation for cooperation, we think is unbelievable and must be rejected. The Prosecution states unequivocally that the accused has not cooperated with the Prosecution. Does Your Honour want me to continue or break now? I saw you looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will break now and come back at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.13 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to make good on the second part of my promise. We received copies of the Yugoslav Criminal Code, and I would like to ask the usher's assistance to distribute it to you. I apologise for, perhaps, a bad copy. It was due to the fact that we received it via fax, but now you have the complete texts of both legislations for your consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we can now listen to Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will just continue with our submission and now discuss the general issue of Mr. Landzo's mental health. The Prosecution has always agreed that this issue is one that is relevant to sentencing, and the Prosecution has accepted that Mr. Landzo has certain personality problems. Indeed, we've suggested from the beginning that this is obvious to anyone who knew anything about his crimes. We suggest, however, that many persons, if not most persons, who commit horrific crimes, such as those committed by Mr. Landzo, have personality difficulties. We do not believe that the circumstances as a whole concerning Mr. Landzo's mental health warrant a significantly reduced sentence. Among other things, we would point out the long period of time over which the crimes occurred in the evidence demonstrating that he had the ability to understand what he was doing was wrong, and he had the full ability to control his actions. Indeed, among other things, we point to the evidence that he frequently initiated mistreatment as evidence that his actions were fully voluntary. During the oral submissions, we heard more evidence from yet another mental health expert. In reviewing his testimony and the testimony of the other mental health experts, I was struck by something I read in Defence Exhibit 90/4, page 297, which is just an article summarising some of what's said about forensic psychiatry, and quoting Dr. Resnik, who indicated that there were five major criticisms made of expert mental health testimony in criminal trials. They were five major criticisms, four of which were that the psychiatrists always disagree, that they speak in jargon-ridden and subjective testimony, that they attempt to dictate the law, and that they give conclusive opinions. The first and, we would suggest, the major criticism is that psychiatrists excuse sin, and we suggest that that is what is attempting to go on here. Every criminal who exhibits sadistic behaviour, such as that exhibited by Mr. Landzo, has problems. Indeed, when Mr. Delic used his electrical device to shock and burn prisoners and laughed while doing so while they begged for mercy, that's also sadistic behaviour. Indeed, one can legitimately argue that when Mr. Mucic amused himself for hours on end by humiliating retarded prisoners, by make them praise Allah, or give details about sexual activities, or dress up as a woman, these are forms of sadistic behaviour, albeit of a lesser form. But any explanation of why Mr. Landzo or any other criminal did what they did, be it dependency or narcissism or transferred aggression, maybe can explain it, but it certainly doesn't excuse it or, in these circumstances, significantly reduce the appropriate punishment. These are just labels. The issue is, could Mr. Landzo understand and control what he was doing? The Prosecution submits that the evidence shows he was in full control of himself, and he did what he wanted to do. He did what was in his interest to do at the time. He chose what to do in Celebici, and he's choosing what he does today, which is to try to manipulate the Court's process to his advantage. But the fact remains, as Mr. Landzo himself recognises at various times, that he needs to be appropriately punished for his horrible crimes. What did, in fact, Dr. Goreta add? Of course, his opinion was preliminary, and he relied, in large part, on the opinions of others, which may be one reason why he didn't differ continually, but they indicated, among other things, that Mr. Landzo could easily choose, for his next role model, a bad person. Dr. Goreta's evidence also indicates that he is very inclined to give recommendations of diminished mental responsibility. Indeed, when asked to review 25 of the most serious cases of war crimes in his own country, he found diminished responsibility in every single one. We would ask that you consider that when you're evaluating his testimony. We note, of course, in the former Yugoslavia, abuse of drugs and alcohol can be a basis of diminished responsibility, and there is evidence that Mr. Landzo voluntarily chose to abuse drugs and alcohol when he was in Celebici. But in almost every country, and we would certainly suggest in this Tribunal, because the taking of such substances are voluntary, they are not used as any kind of basis for diminished responsibility. We certainly suggest that Your Honours should not allow that here. Of course, as Dr. Goreta pointed out when he was asked about his tendency to find diminished responsibility, he said, "Well, this is just my recommendation. The courts in Yugoslavia do not have to accept it." In fact, we don't know how many times it was accepted, but certainly before this Tribunal, this Court does not have to substitute the judgement of a psychiatrist for its own judgement, and we would suggest, based on the evidence as a whole and common sense, there is no reason to significantly reduce Mr. Landzo's sentence because of any mental health difficulties. The Defence then goes on, I think, related at another portion of their brief to claim that Mr. Landzo has been rehabilitated. This is, in our submission, also unbelievable in all senses of the word. The Defence has presented much evidence that Mr. Landzo has long-standing problems, problems and, indeed, a tendency, and that he did engage in violent behaviour, both before and after he was in Celebici. Given the fact that one can't control what he does out in society, we would certainly suggest he remains a danger. Similarly, apparently, as part of his rehabilitation, the Defence now tries to claim that Mr. Landzo is remorseful, but we ask you to consider what actual evidence of remorse is there and when and under what circumstances has it come about? Mr. Landzo has said in his statement that he wants to apologise to the victims, but, of course, a number of the victims were here, and there was no attempt to apologise. In fact, the Defence attacked the witnesses. In fact, Mr. Landzo himself threatened a witness. When Mr. Landzo testified that he tried to get money from his attorney, that wasn't money for the victims of his crime, that wasn't money for the families of the people he killed who now have no means of livelihood, that was money for Mr. Landzo and his own people. When he testified, was there evidence of genuine remorse? We suggest that there was absolutely none. It appears that this remorse has just appeared after the presentation of the Defence and after his testimony and only in connection with his sentencing proceedings. We suggest that Mr. Landzo's expressions of remorse in which he says, "I am remorseful," is yet another straightforward attempt to manipulate events to his own advantage. We also suggest that in evaluating his rehabilitation, his remorse, his wanting to take responsibility for what he's done, we look closely at his written statement in which he describes much of his life in great detail, except when you get to the part about Celebici, and he says, "I did what I could to protect my country and no one is perfect." The Prosecution submitted it's unbelievable that someone who, for months on end, killed or tortured or sexual assaulted people --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I suggest there's not been any evidence of sexual assault --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear your submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In respectful submission of the Prosecution, Mr. Landzo, who has admitted that he forced brothers to commit fellatio with each other would certainly be encompassed as sexual assault. When asked about his conduct or when describing his conduct, all he can say is, "Well, no one is perfect." Continuing with the Defence submission, the Defence then asked that whatever sentence that Mr. Landzo gets, he should get credit for the time he served in Bosnia for what is referred to here as the Bubulo case. This is, frankly, also ludicrous. Mr. Landzo wants credit for time served for another murder that he committed which isn't even charged here or part of this case. The Defence then suggests, in their written submissions, that Mr. Landzo has been the victim of selective prosecution. I believe that as Your Honours have already noted, this is not a matter for this Chamber, much less a sentencing matter, but I must go further and suggest that this argument is not only unbelievable and unsupported, it's offensive, as is the idea that his crimes are not serious enough to be before this Tribunal. Mr. Landzo's final argument in their written submissions is that his sentence should reflect only his mistreatment of eight detainees. This is ridiculous, it's undisputed, even by Mr. Landzo that he mistreated, in horrible ways, many, many, detainees. Indeed, it would be impossible for any indictment to include, individually, every single act of mistreatment committed by Mr. Landzo in the Celebici camp. There are just too many. Even he --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What type of argument is it? Why don't you let her make her argument? Everything that has been said is the evidence which is before the Trial Chamber, and you keep objecting to what has been said in the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: There are just too many acts of mistreatment to describe individually. The indictment specifically charges Mr. Landzo with inhumane conditions, including the creation of an atmosphere of terror created by his numerous acts of mistreatment. His sentence for the count of inhumane conditions should reflect the enormity of what he did to the detainees in the camp. Indeed, even if this were the only charge in the indictment, in view of the Prosecution, Mr. Landzo would deserve a life sentence. In sum, Your Honours, under all the circumstances, including the number of persons personally killed by Mr. Landzo, the number of persons personally tortured by Mr. Landzo, and the hundreds of persons who are subjected to various forms of mistreatment, including living for months in an atmosphere of terror, the Prosecution believes that Mr. Landzo should receive a life sentence. The Prosecution also suggests, for the reasons articulated in detail in the Tadic judgement, which I will not describe in detail, that Your Honours give a recommendation concerning the minimum amount of years that an accused should serve. We submit that Your Honours should recommend that under no circumstances should Mr. Landzo be released in less than 25 years. Let me now, please, turn to Mr. Delic. My argument on Mr. Delic will be shorter, not because his conduct is less serious, to the contrary, but because his arguments are fewer and generally are not arguments of mitigation, but are, generally, legal arguments that have previously been rejected before this Tribunal. Mr. Delic's first argument is that any sentence more than 15 years is illegal and a violation of the nullen crimin principle. We would first point out that given the former Yugoslavia had the death penalty, any lesser sentence, including life imprisonment, cannot be a violation of nullen crimen. Further, in Erdemovic 1, the Erdemovic Chamber expressly considered the nullen crimen argument and rejected it. Although it's not binding on this Court, there is nothing in the appellate decision or the subsequent Erdemovic judgement to cast doubt on the reasoning. Finally, we would note that the Tadic Chamber implicitly rejected this argument in sentencing Mr. Tadic to greater than 15 years. Mr. Delic, as part of this, has made a number of arguments concerning the sentencing in the former Yugoslavia and, indeed, I believe we had pretty much a whole day of testimony on this. As stated in its submission, the Prosecution believes that of other Chambers in this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal have found, the practice in the former Yugoslavia is not binding upon this Chamber in any event, and there are a number of reasons for this. One, as found by the Tadic and Erdemovic Chambers, the main goals of punishment may differ in International Tribunals. Another problem is determining what the practice is. The Tadic Chamber received reports in evidence, which we believe Your Honours can take judicial notice of, concerning the details of the practice in the former Yugoslavia. In some respect, those details differ from that presented by Mr. Tomic, but we would suggest, in any event, it's not the details that are important. Certainly, it is clear that in war crimes and other serious crimes, including homicides such as occurred in Celebici --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. I was reading in Article 24 -- I was looking at Article 24, clause 1, in determining the term of imprisonment, the Trial Chamber shall have recourse to the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To have recourse. You must look at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have always said and we said in our written submission, and I believe all the Chambers before this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal have had recourse, meaning to look to for guidance, but have stated that it is not binding, that it may be instructive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is meant as having a recourse, as in resorting to, referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We believe that it may be a reference and that it may be a guide. Let me just try to find the quote, on pages 5 and 6 of our written submission, among other things, in the first Erdemovic decision, the Court found: "The Trial Chamber considers that the reference to this practice," the practice in the former Yugoslavia, "Can be used for guidance but is not binding."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just thinking out loud, I thought when it said "recourse" that it means more than guidance. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would suggest that recourse does not, by its plain language, indicate that it's more than a guide or a reference, and as the Erdemovic Chamber found and as the Kambanda case in Rwanda found, and the Rwanda Statute has an identical reference, that the International Tribunal for Rwanda shall have recourse to the sentencing practices in Rwanda. In both those cases, the courts found that such practices are not binding, and the word "recourse" is not meant to indicate that they are binding, but such practices are one of the factors to be taken into account. One reason for that, as one reason I've already mentioned, is the difficulty in determining exactly what the practice is. Another reason articulated by the Chambers is that the main goals of punishment may differ, appropriately, between this International Tribunal and other Tribunals. Going back, though, to the practice in the former Yugoslavia, because we certainly agree that it is relevant, it is clear that in war crimes and in serious crimes such as homicide, an accused could receive a sentence of death or 20 years or lesser terms of imprisonment. It's also clear that a court did not have to impose a death penalty before pronouncing a 20-year sentence but could just prove a 20-year sentence. It's also clear that courts gave the death sentence infrequently. One expert said, approximately, two times a year, and the expert, Mr. Tomic, here said less and only in extremely hard cases. 20-year sentences, however, were given more frequently and were not so limited. The main factor in the practice in the former Yugoslavia, we believe, is not in dispute and, indeed, Mr. Tomic finally agreed to it, which was very accurately and succinctly summarised in one sentence by the Tadic court, which is "Imprisonment as a form of punishment was limited to a term of 15 years or in cases for which the death penalty was prescribed as an alternative to imprisonment to a term of 20 years." Mr. Delic then renews his legal argument, this is in his written submissions, that he has been improperly charged with both 7(1) and 7(3), responsibility, both participation and superior responsibility. The Defence has suggested that the responsibility under 7(1) and 7(3) are mutually exclusive and, in fact, alternative charges. The Prosecution contends that they are not alternative and that an accused may be found guilty under both theories of responsibility. In this case, the accused, Mr. Delic, had multiple roles and, in our submission, has been properly charged with responsibility for his multiple roles. I would point out that it is often the case that an accused can be found guilty under multiple theories of responsibility, particularly in cases here where you have a superior and his subordinates engaged in a crime. In such cases, a superior can and should be responsible for both his own direct participation and for his actions and omissions regarding his subordinates. Different interests are being protected in the scope of the charges, and the ultimate sentence should certainly reflect those different interests. As noted by the Tadic court, when asked to decide whether certain accounts are cumulative rather than alternative, and I'll just make it clear for Mr. Moran that I'm quoting, I believe, from the Tadic decision, since I know he gets upset when the Prosecution uses the word "technicality." As the Tadic court found, an accused's ultimate sentence will not depend on a technicalities pleading, but rather on proven criminal conduct. In this case, Your Honours could probably find Mr. Delic guilty, both of those crimes with which he was a direct participant and those counts charging superior responsibility. Your Honours could, if you believe it appropriate, merge those convictions for purposes of sentencing. Alternatively, if Your Honours wish, you could find Mr. Delic guilty of those crimes with which he was a direct participant and then exclude just those murders from the superior responsibility counts with respect to him but find him guilty of superior responsibility for the other murders. In any case, in arriving at his ultimate sentence, Mr. Delic's sentence should be greater to reflect his multiple responsibilities for the crimes. In his submission concerning an appropriate sentence, Mr. Delic then goes on to suggest that, in this Tribunal, the protection of society in the deterrence effect does not warrant a long sentence for any -- the protection of society does not warrant a long sentence for any accused, including himself. The Prosecution would disagree and note, among other things, that Bosnia-Herzegovina may likely have ethnic tensions for a long period of time and in different areas. Certain groups may continue to be a minority and be in a position to be victimised. That's why it's important that, in addition to the legitimate goal of retribution, sentences for war crimes Tribunals should be intended to deter and, indeed, Chambers in this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal have noted that these retribution and deterrence are the most important goals at arriving at just sentences before this Tribunal. The Delic Defence suggests that the only deterrence that should be considered relevant is that of superiors. We would first note that, in fact, Mr. Delic has been charged with superior responsibility, but on a more general level, the Prosecution rejects categorically, the idea that this Tribunal should only be concerned with deterring superiors. To the contrary. It is crucial that all participants in a war, be they superiors or common foot soldiers, understand that the laws of war mean something and that everyone can be held accountable for their crimes. To suggest that the conduct of individual soldiers or guards, all of whom have the power of life and death over others, may not be influenced, or it's not important to influence them is, in our view, fundamentally wrong and fundamentally against one of the reasons why this Tribunal was created. The Defence then finally suggests in its written submission, including the attachments, that on a few occasions Mr. Delic assisted some detainees or their families, and the Defence reports once in November of 1992 when mistreatment was still continuing, Mr. Delic interrupted a beating of a prisoner by other guards and allowed the prisoner to return to the hangar. The Defence also reports that Mr. Delic once arranged for some soap to be given to the prisoners. The Prosecution does not contest these incidents, but believes that under the totality of the circumstances, they are of little or no significance. As noted by the Chamber in the Mummothey case and cited in the Prosecution's closing brief, "It is not an unusual phenomena in life to find an isolated good deed emerging from an evil man, because of convenience, caprice, or even a sudden gleam of benevolence forcing its way through a callused heart, even a murderer can help a child to safety." Mr. Delic was a murderer, he was a torturer, he was a rapist. He horribly mistreated numerous detainees. Mr. Delic did these things himself and he ordered others to do so. I emphasise again that the evidence that Mr. Delic ordered others to mistreat detainees was witnessed by a large number of victims who testified, and there is no need to rely solely on Mr. Landzo's testimony concerning this. As a superior, Mr. Delic did everything possible to foster an environment where others could and did mistreat detainees on their own initiative with no consequence. The detainees lived in deathly fear of Mr. Delic. I think it is almost impossible for us to comprehend the enormity of the power exercised by Mr. Delic, the suffering caused by his actions and his omissions, and the deprived nature of his conduct. Of course, there are no significant mitigating factors relating to Mr. Delic, including the lack of any remorse. Mr. Delic's sentence should reflect the enormity of his crimes as participant and as superior. In the recommendation of the Prosecution, Mr. Delic should receive a life sentence. In the recommendation of the Prosecution, the Chamber's verdict should also recommend that under no circumstances should Mr. Delic be released before 30 years. Unless Your Honours have any additional questions about Mr. Landzo or Mr. Delic, Mr. Niemann will now speak about Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delalic and respond to their submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document which was submitted this morning regarding the written statement by Mrs. Delic should be numbered D112/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If the Court pleases. Your Honours, I'm dealing first with the written submission submitted to Your Honours in relation to the accused Zejnil Delalic. Your Honours, I go through this submission and address the various issues, some of the various issues raised there. Some of them have been adequately dealt with, either in our written brief or in the course of the proceedings, and I don't think bear repetition, but there are some matters I think, Your Honours, that may be appropriate for me to discuss in the course of this submission. First and foremost, on the first page of the written submission of the accused Zejnil Delalic, we are assured that the information that's provided in this submission, in this written submission, is intended for the purposes of sentence only. I make reference to that, Your Honours, because it would seem that when you go further into the submission, that we see that matters which were raised also as part of his Defence would appear to have been raised as part of mitigation of the penalty. I just draw that distinction, that it seems that in the case of this submission, those matters are being raised again for that purpose. To some extent, I will touch upon them very briefly to deal with the aspect of them being raised in mitigation. Your Honours, on page 6 of their submission, they draw attention to the fact that in keeping with general observations on sentencing, the sentencing of an accused person who is convicted of having superior responsibility must be determined on a case-by-case basis, according to the circumstances of each case. We don't refute that, Your Honours. We fully accept that the case-by-case analysis is an essential feature of any sentencing process. But in saying that, Your Honours, we submit that, although the case-by-case analysis is an important part, one should not lose sight of the general principles that apply in sentencing and in sentencing a superior in this case. Your Honours, questions arise when it comes to sentencing of superiors, such as should the sentence of the superior be less than a subordinate? Is it appropriate that the subordinate receives a greater sentence than the subordinate? After all, it can be argued that the subordinate is carrying out the wishes of the superior, that he's carrying out the orders of the superior. The superior has an objective that he wants to achieve, and he uses the subordinate in the role of facilitator in order to carry it out. So the superior has the responsibility to ensure that the acts of the subordinate are carried out in order to achieve his or her objective. That is a general principle, Your Honour, that must apply in our respectful submission, and so one must assume from that that the superior knows what he wishes to achieve when he sets out to obtain a purpose. If the subordinate is merely carrying out those wishes, then is it appropriate that the subordinate receive the greater sentence? Indeed, I think that it's this rational that goes behind the principle that superior orders are a mitigating factor. They are not a Defence, but a mitigating factor. In our submission, Your Honours, one starts with the proposition that the superior sentence should be greater than the sentence of the subordinate, and it's only that when one looks at the case-by-case basis that do you then seek or do you then proceed, if necessary, to mitigate the sentence. As I said, some of the issues that were raised by Mr. Delalic in his submission are matters that go to his Defence as well, but can be legitimately raised by way of mitigation. I'm not going to repeat all of them, but on page 7 of Mr. Delalic's submission, he raises the fact that, first of all, he wasn't present when a lot of the crimes were committed. Well, Your Honours, what this means is that it may be the case that he wasn't there at the immediate time the crime was committed, so he may not have been in a position to take immediate action. He may not have known the full details of the events in the way that an eyewitness may have seen it. But then, Your Honours, we must ask the question what steps did he take to prevent things from happening when he knew, ultimately, that they occurred. One of the next matters that is put is that he didn't know in advance. Again, this may be so, but, Your Honours, if there is a continuing course of criminal conduct going over a significant period of time, it's strange to suggest that he never knew at any stage. In our submission, Your Honours, on the first occasion, if he didn't know in advance, that may be a matter which would be the basis of some mitigation of the penalty, not entirely, because a supervisor has the responsibility to put in train, means whereby he will be informed, or means whereby these crimes themselves will not be committed. Your Honours, in relation to that, it's true that not being present and not knowing in advance may have some mitigating benefit for him in sentence. It's interesting, Your Honours, when one looks at Exhibit P116, which is the interview on television. It's a video interview on television. Mr. Delalic is specifically asked about the Celebici camp and the conditions that are said to prevail there, and he says that, "It's only TV Belgrade which says it's notorious," and then he refers to the fact that organisations such as the Red Cross had been there, and he says, "The people are detained in the barracks. Their rights and conditions are as was possible in such accommodation. Their relatives can visit them. They have regular meals. I think they are better fed than our soldiers." Your Honours, he certainly knew something about the conditions at the camp at the time so that he was in a position to speak of those events at that time. It's also been raised on page 8 of their submission the fact that the conditions in Celebici and, no doubt, the Konjic area in general, were hard at the time. Having regard to the conditions that prevailed, they did their best. Your Honours, this isn't, in our submission, either a Defence or a plea in mitigation. The position is, Your Honours, that if you wish to take prisoners of war or civilians and put them into camps and restrain them there, then, Your Honours, you are obliged, under the Geneva Conventions, to ensure that the conditions that are prescribed by those conventions are maintained. But irrespective of whether there are minor breaches of the Geneva Conventions, there are such vis-à-vis the conditions that apply. There was no necessity for these people to be kept in tunnels, to be deprived of water when water was available, for them to be beaten and so forth. On page 9, Your Honours, they go on in their submissions to make reference to the fact that the detainees were arrested in conformity with the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In our submission, Your Honours, there is no basis for this at all. There's nothing that emerges from the evidence that suggests that is so. We have no evidence at all that people were notified of their charges. We have no evidence at all that they were taken expeditiously before a judge. We have no evidence at all that they were given access to legal counsel. We have no evidence at all that they had such rights as discovery or trial or sentence or anything. All we now, Your Honours, is that they --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, Your Honours, this treatment is, in no way, consistent with someone who is being legally arrested and detained. They also go on and speak of Mr. Delalic intervening in a personal capacity to attempt to secure the release of certain individuals. Your Honours, what this demonstrates, in our submission, is that he had the capacity and the authority in Celebici to take steps to release certain prisoners, should he decide to do so. There is then on page 10 of their submission, a reference to the aim of the military action of the JNA, et cetera. That was to eliminate the institutions of legal government and to destroy Bosniaks and Croats. Your Honours, when it comes to this whole issue, what has been ignored by this is that there was, in fact, a process of transition going on between the breakdown of the federal state of Yugoslavia and the emergence of the independent sovereign states, among others, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and so forth. There were people contained in Bosnia-Herzegovina who took a different political point of view, who desired to be ruled by alternative political masters and who sought to maintain their territory for that purpose. So we're not assisted much, nor does it amount to mitigation, for it to be suggested that somehow what was happening in Konjic, by the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the only legitimate course available. Then it goes on on page 12 as an extension of this argument to suggest that the reason why the people were placed in Celebici was to put down what amounts to an armed rebellion. Having regard to the two views that were prevailing in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that relevant time, a similar argument could be relevantly advanced in relations to people detained in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Your Honours, we are not assisted in any way, by these comparisons, nor do they amount, in our submission, to a mitigation. What is significant is to examine the conditions that prevailed there, to look at the people who were responsible for the particular institutions, be they Celebici, Omarska, Keraterm, or whatever, and to determine whether or not, having regard to the conditions that prevailed, there has been a breach of the Geneva Conventions in terms of the conditions, or whether other crimes against humanity have been committed. On page 14 of the submission of Zejnil Delalic, in relation to a submission made under the heading of "Activities of Delalic from April to November 1992," the submission speaks of the fact that Mr. Delalic was absent from time to time. They specifically speak of him being absent in May when he was in Zagreb. They speak of his activities in relation to the railway that was being constructed between Pazaric and Jablanica. Your Honours, these are matters which were reflected in the documents that were recovered by the Austrian police in Vienna and confirm, Your Honours, the very matters which the Defence now seek to rely upon as a matter of mitigation. On page 18 of their submission, the Defence of Zejnil Delalic said that he has given substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor, and in support of that, they cite the two records of interviews in which he participated in. Your Honours, the mere giving of a record of interview is not, of itself, evidence of cooperation with the Prosecution. Certainly, there are circumstances when it can be, but it's not some automatic thing that flows as a consequence of giving a record of interview. It can be given for the purposes of advancing their Defence. It can be given for the purposes of endeavouring to persuade the Prosecution not to proceed with the charges. In the case of the record of interview of Mr. Delalic, it's the Prosecution's contention that, in some cases, he was evasive and, in other cases, where he spoke of the War Presidency having responsibilities and being in charge, we see when it comes to the trial that this, what we say, true and correct position, was abandoned in favour of some other confusing formulation inconsistent with what he said in his record of interview. The Prosecution says, Your Honours, that the accused, Zejnil Delalic, has given no cooperation to the Prosecution at all. If he had given cooperation to the Prosecution, we certainly would have acknowledged it. It would have been a matter which would have advanced the Prosecution's task, either generally in relation to this Tribunal or in connection with this case. It's our submission that there is nothing that can be pointed to by the accused, Zejnil Delalic, to say that he has cooperated with the Prosecution. On that basis, in our submission, Your Honour, there's no basis for him to seek mitigation of the penalty on that account. There's also a reference to the fact that the accused, Zejnil Delalic, provided the Prosecution with numerous documents. Again, this is a decision that's made on a tactical basis by his counsel for a whole host of reasons and do not automatically point to the fact that this amounts to a mitigation of the penalty. In our submission, Your Honours, neither of those matters give rise or justification to that basis. There has been and there is, in this submission on page 22, a sort of, justification, for what occurred in Celebici made out on the basis that, well, how bad it may have been, it wasn't as bad as what happened in places like Omarska. Well, I repeat and echo what I said earlier in relation to that, but I add to it, that there's no evidence before Your Honours at all about what happened in Omarska. There's no evidence whatsoever what happened in the other camps. The evidence before Your Honours is in relation only to the Celebici camp. In our submission, Your Honours, you're not assisted, in any way, by that submission. Your Honours, we heard in relation to the evidence called concerning the character of the accused, Zejnil Delalic, that he had a moderate attitude towards people of different ethnic backgrounds and, in particular, I recall the evidence that he didn't refer to people by name such as "Chetniks" or other. I remind Your Honours of Exhibit P116. Again, it's the television interview which is on video where one sees the accused, Zejnil Delalic, speaking and where, in describing the military actions that are going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant time, he speaks in terms of the Chetniks, their tanks, and so forth. I don't need to actually quote it in detail, Your Honours. It's there to be seen. In our submission, it's not correct to say that that was the situation, that he would never use such terms. Your Honours, in line with what my colleague, Ms. McHenry, has said in terms of the Prosecutor's recommendations, having regard to the role that he played, having regard to matters that he has raised in mitigation, it's the recommendation of the Prosecution that the sentence in this case should be a sentence of 10 years. I now turn, Your Honours, to the submissions made by the defendant Mucic. Again, I will go through the written submissions and address just some of the issues that have been raised. Mr. Mucic says on page 5 of his submissions concerning the general question of sentencing that, and I think it's better I read it, "Modern jurisprudence is tending to come away from sentencing policy based upon retribution and or deterrence and to concentrate on education and protection as an alternative." My colleague, Ms. McHenry, has taken you to what was said in the Tadic case about this. It's my understanding of the modern trends in sentencing that this is not the case at all, that rehabilitation has been found not to work and that the principle of the penalty being made to fit the crime, sometimes described as just deserves, is the appropriate basis upon which sentencing should be approached. I say it in particular relation to this Tribunal, because there may be a legitimate national interest in countries pursuing a policy of rehabilitation where those countries believe that rehabilitation will be effective in reducing recidivism and will benefit the community as a whole. This Tribunal is in no position, Your Honours, to supervise sentenced persons during the period of time that they serve their sentence. The Tribunal has a limited life in which it is to deal with and address the issues in the former Yugoslavia, and that the significant issue is that persons accused and brought before this Tribunal and convicted of the crimes charged, be sentenced in order that justice be done and that the sentence that is imposed should amount to appropriate sentence, having regard to the justice of the matter. Your Honours, on page 11 in their submission, it said that, in speaking of Mr. Mucic, that if a number of offenders are being sentenced together, the fact that other defendants might be thought to be deserving of a more substantial overall custodial sentence than Mr. Mucic, it doesn't automatically mean that he should receive a longer sentence. Your Honours, the individual culpability includes his position as a superior. In his own evidence, Your Honours, he was able to ameliorate conditions in Musala, according to the attachments, that there is absolutely no reason why he couldn't have done the same thing in Celebici. He knew what was happening in Celebici. He could have taken action to stop it. His acquiescence, in our submission, was seen as a sign of his approval. He is more culpable, Your Honours, than the mere guard who is instructed to carry something out and does do it. In our submission, Your Honours, if a superior receives a light sentence or receives a lesser sentence than subordinates who are merely carrying out the wishes of the superiors, then this, in the eyes of not only the subordinates but the wider community, could be seen as an injustice, unless, again, it can be justified on the basis of valid and appropriate mitigating factors. Again, in my submission, Your Honours, one must look at the general principle, and only after that, one decides whether or not the sentence should be mitigated to something less than what the subordinate receives, if the mitigation so deserves. On page 12, there are a number of mitigating factors set out in their submission. They make reference, firstly, to the previous good character of the accused. Your Honours, before this Tribunal, the previous good character of persons, especially persons who are in superior positions, is likely to be the rule, rather than the exception. Indeed, for superiors and people in higher positions who are charged in relation to these types of crimes, it's probably going to be exceptional that they will have a bad prior criminal record or a previous bad character. The next submission put to Your Honours on page 12 is the lack of participation in direct acts of unlawful behaviour. Your Honours, it's easy to have one's feelings aroused by terrible stories of cruelty and torture being inflicted upon innocent human beings who are kept in circumstances of captivity, and for one to determine a sentence based on the reaction that one has to those sorts of descriptions, but that behaviour, in most of the cases that have come before this Tribunal, will be carried out by the subordinate, while the superior either turns a blind eye, is not present, or fails to intervene. But, again, Your Honours must ask the question, "Who is more culpable in these circumstances?" The next issue of mitigation that is urged upon Your Honours is the inevitable psychological effect and long-term confinement and detrimental effects upon the defendant and his immediate family. Your Honours, the effects of a crime upon an accused and his immediate family are the inevitable consequences of the crime. They are not a mitigating factor, in my respectful submission, at all. They are the consequences of the crime itself. Once Your Honours determine that the accused has committed the crime, then, yes, there will be this impact, and it will affect his immediate family, and one can feel tragedy for it, but it is not a mitigating factor. It's an inevitable consequence. Your Honours, then it is said in his submission that the particular feature that incarceration in a country and a culture, to the defendant, is a factor that makes such incarceration more difficult and more punitive for any individual. Well, that is a submission made in a vacuum. What is it really saying? It's saying to Your Honours, "Well, he's going to be in a country away from his home, and it may be in a gaol which is less than as good as he might expect in his own country or somewhere else." At this stage, Your Honours don't have any idea where his incarceration will take place, so it's quite impossible for you to determine a sentence on the basis that he may go to some place which has better gaol facilities than others or have better conditions relating to the treatment of prisoners than others. Again, Your Honours, this is an issue that goes close to the question of rehabilitation. The whole question is, does the sentence that's imposed upon the accused adequately reflect the offending that has occurred, and is it just in those circumstances. Your Honours really cannot hope to deal with that question, because you simply don't know where the accused will end up. It's suggested on page 13 of the submission that there's no credible evidence of active, direct participation to a person in respect of any of the violence or inhumane treatment. Your Honours, there's lots of evidence of his participation in the inhumane treatment. He was there. He saw the conditions. He could have done something about it. He didn't do anything about it. He knew that people were being put down holes and incarcerated in these totally unacceptable horrific circumstances, and he didn't do anything about it. To that extent, he certainly participated, Your Honours. There's some evidence put before you that he assisted others in escaping. Again, I say this is evidence of the fact that he was in a position to do something about it, could have done, but didn't, in relation to the other unfortunate persons that were left behind. Your Honours, there was also mention in relation to Mr. Mucic about the fact that he wouldn't engage in referring to people by derogatory terms and that he had an even and balanced attitude to all ethnic groups. To balance that, Your Honours, I encourage you to, again, look at the videotape of Exhibit P110 that was mentioned by my colleague, Ms. McHenry, in her submission, where Your Honours see, at length, where Mr. Mucic has before him a Serb prisoner and where he humiliates that person and forces him to sing verses and quote animal names and so forth. In relation to the question of whether or not he uses those terms, there is a passage in that where Mr. Mucic is speaking to this prisoner, and he says, "Raise the pistol higher. Raise your arms. Are you a Chetnik, Risto?" Your Honours can see that for yourself. In our submission, Your Honours, the accused Mujic knew what was happening in the camp. He was in a position of responsibility. He could have done something about it. He knew it was wrong. He sought the people being tormented and humiliated. We have even some video evidence of this, not that one would have ever expected to see that. He could have acted. He failed to act. In our submission, Your Honours, the appropriate sentence in these circumstances is a sentence of 20 years imprisonment. Those are our submissions, Your Honours, unless I can help you with any other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In which order is the Defence making its submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're doing it in the order of the indictment, but I'm not sure. We're not?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'll be happy to do it in the order of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think we are doing it in the order we presented evidence. I have a submission to the Court, if we can take our break 20 minutes early and shorten it a little bit, from a half hour break, to break now, and then come back at 4.00, and then go right through until we're done, because it might keep things in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If we do it now and we come back at 4.00, that means we may not break until 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be, personally, a little shocked if we were still here at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's the only alternative. If we continue now and break at 4.00, then it means we come back at 4.30 and then until 5.30. But if we break now, we will come back at 4.00 and continue until 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To some extent, I think it's six to one and half a dozen to another, but whatever pleases the Court. I was thinking that we could do it now and maybe shorten it for a few minutes because we only got two accused here today, and then just continue on without a break. That's my own suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I go along with Tom Moran. If you aren't prepared to take a lengthy break at this time, I would ask to be excused for about three minutes, since it appears we are going in the order of sentencing and that I will be up first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will break now and come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Has the Defence decided as to which way you're giving the submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I thought we were going to go in the order we presented evidence, but I see there's one person missing in action, and in light of that, I'll go first. I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good. Then they can join in when they come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is probably the 100th time I've stood behind this podium, during this trial, and it's going to be the last time, I hope. The next time we're all assembled here, the Court's going to be delivering its judgement, and the only thing I am going to do is stand up when the Trial Chamber announces your judgement. What I'm going to do this afternoon is first, right off, talk about a very few things that the Prosecutor said. I'll probably take about two minutes on that or three minutes on that, and then I have a few other things I want to say. The Prosecutor, Ms. McHenry, talked about people being entitled to a lower sentence. Nobody is entitled to sentences. That's for Judges to decide. Judges, in the exercise of your discretion and your wisdom, viewing all of the facts. She says your expecting majority of the sentences will be severe. If that, in fact, was what the Security Council had in mind when this Tribunal was created, then in Article 24(1), they could have said the minimum sentence would be 10 years or 20 years or 50 years or whatever. That's not correct. The whole range of punishment, from no punishment at all to whatever is available under the Statute, we've talked about the issues of legality and nullen crimin. I talked about that at length in writing, you will read it. I'm not going to talk about it anymore. I have presented a little bit of evidence on mental health. I think that we need to clear something up. Mental health information can go to two different things. One is whether or not a person is guilty of a crime. If a person is insane, a person is not guilty of a crime. The other thing you can look at is how does a person's mental health status affect what the Court should do in assessing punishment. I've presented mental health evidence that I've had, as you can see from the date, in my possession for over a year. It helps you learn more about Mr. Hazim Delic, to help you exercise your discretion. How did Mr. Delic get into custody? It's pretty straightforward. He got a call from the ministry of the interior, the MUP, to report to Sarajevo, and he went into custody. Yes, there was a delay on getting him to the Tribunal, and one of the delays may very well have been caused by the fact that he is misidentified in the indictment. He has the wrong date of birth. Paragraph 4 in the indictment shows his date of birth as May 13, 1964. His actual date of birth is May 14, 1960. The jurisdiction that I'm familiar with wants to be darn sure if you are going to be extraditing somebody, you have the right guy. This Tribunal already has some experience on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Were there any other persons by the name of Hazim Delic in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And no one is suggesting that. I'm just suggesting that it's a problem with identifying as a legal matter. It's a decision that lawyers make. He reported to Sarajevo. He was reported where he was told to report and he was taken into custody. He didn't go into hiding, go running across borders, anything like that. The Prosecutor likes citing Erdemovic 1. It's been overruled by the Appeals Chamber. It's clearly not binding. If you want to look at it, fine, but it's not authority. It's overruled. She asked you to take judicial notice of evidence in the Tadic case. I would ask you not to do that, and the reason I would ask you not to do that is that no one has ever given it to me. I don't know what it is. My client clearly ought to, at least, know what the evidence against him is and I ought to know that. We talked about the principles of legality, and Judge Jan, especially, I think you were asking about Article 24(1) of the Statute, and looking at Yugoslav practice. I think we have to draw a distinction. I've raised two issues. Dr. Tomic, in his testimony, raised two issues. One is the issue of legality, that is, prior to the time this Tribunal was created as an enforcement mechanism, is the maximum punishment limited to what was available under Yugoslav law? The other half of that -- that's a legal question. The other half of that is look at the practice to get a feel for what the Yugoslav courts did, and that's -- the United Nations, the Security Council told you to do that. It's not binding on you. One, if I'm correct, may be binding. The other is something to help you in the exercise of your discretion. I looked through the indictment again today, and I didn't see any counts on genocide and war crimes. In the Erdemovic appeals decision, the Appeals Chamber made it clear that genocide and the war crimes are the most serious offensives. I may be misquoting the Court and if I am I apologise. Ordinary war crimes are less severe because they do not attack humanity as a whole. I think the Court needs to keep that in consideration. Article 7(1) and 7(3) liability. Article 7(1) is a crime of commission. You do something, you order it, you do it yourself. You're an aider and abettor. Article 7(3) is crimes of omission. You didn't do something. I don't know how you can be sentenced of both. Ms. McHenry said my client showed no remorse. Well, as a practical matter, my client has pled not guilty. My client has told the Prosecutor to prove it, and the Trial Chamber has not yet decided whether or not the Prosecutor has proved it. I couldn't let a client get up here and say, "I'm not guilty yet and I'm pleading not guilty, but I'm sure sorry for all those things I did." Under the procedure we're using, it would just be essentially changing the plea to guilty, and it's something that neither the Prosecutor, nor the Trial Chamber, should expect. With that, almost every time I've stood up before here in the past to argue things, I've been arguing the law. To me, the law is a very important thing, and I think we had to focus on it in the past. Every time I've done that, I've tried to be honest with the Trial Chamber on what I think the law is, if it's clear, and if it's not clear, what I think it ought to be, and to draw the distinction between the two. But that's an intellectual exercise. Right now, I've thought about this, and I may not be as articulate as I would like to be, but right now is a time for me to talk to you and talk to you from my heart about what I feel. You have to decide the facts about what occurred in Celebici. But if you decide those facts adverse to my client, you're going to arrive at a sentencing decision. First, let me say that there is no one in this building that has more respect for the law of war than I do. I just added it up today, 23 days, two months, and 23 days wearing a uniform. I taught people about this. I care about it. I think it's important. If I didn't think the law of war was important, I wouldn't be here. Now, having said that, all war crimes aren't the same. You can look at a situation, the Einsatz group, in cases where people went out and deliberately engaged in horrible murders and war crimes as a matter of policy. You have war crimes that are ordered or condoned by high officials. I would submit that those are more significant and they are worse and should be punished more than crimes that are not of that type, that are not the organised, deliberate crimes against humanity and genocide. In assessing punishment, I think you need to look at a lot of things. One of the things I think you need to look at is the training and background of the offender. Another thing you have to look at is the surrounding facts. In my written submission, I referred to, I believe it's, eight factors that General Peers found in his investigation of a US Army atrocity during Vietnam, and I'm not going to go through those factors with you on things where there is a heightened possibility of war crimes. What we have here, let's look at the surroundings of Celebici, and if the Trial Chamber believes, beyond a reasonable doubt, these things happened, I'm not using this for an excuse, I'm just saying it's something that should be considered in setting punishment. It's clear from all of the evidence that not only these four defendants, two here, but the other two, they didn't have any training in the jobs they were in. Esad Landzo testified he was basically handed a uniform and a rifle and said, "Go be a guard." Hazim Delic didn't have any training in any kind of leadership. The guy was an assembly line worker. Pavo Mucic, he is not a trained military officer, trained leader. Zejnil Delalic, he's a businessman. He's not a general officer. We're not dealing with the Coldstream guards here. We're dealing with a bunch of people who were thrown into a situation without being trained to deal with the situation they were in. All of us that have come from places where we're dealing with everything from soldiers to police officers, to prison guards. We train them so that they will know you don't do these things, and they will have the discipline not to do those things. None of these people had that. The kind of fighting you had, this was neighbour versus neighbour. This was a brutal, bitter war, and it takes training and supervision from the highest level down to the lowest level to keep people from doing what they want to do. Finally, let's look at the facilities at Celebici for a second, that place right over there. That's not a prison. That's a warehouse. For reasons unknown to me, unknown, as far as I know, everyone in this room, that was selected as a prison. People like Hazim Delic had to try to work within that. Am I saying that it's the kind of thing I would pick for a prison if I were selecting and I had the ability to select? No. I'm not saying that at all. But all of those factors have to go into the consideration of what sentence to give in the event that there's a conviction. None of these people here, especially my client, were traffic policemen that drove 50 miles so that they could go to a prison camp and torture and murder people just for the fun of it. No one is suggesting that. Mr. Niemann hasn't suggested that. No one has suggested it here. These were people that were put in a bad situation, and maybe they didn't make the best of it, but it lacks the inherent -- I'm not being articulate here today. I can't even think of the right word. But it's something, I think, of a different magnitude. Post-traumatic stress syndrome, you've heard more about post-traumatic stress syndrome than you ever want to here.
