Dr. Prince told you that Mr. Delic suffers from post-traumatic stress syndrome. Nobody is asking you to use that to exclude any criminal culpability or criminal responsibility that you find. If you find, beyond a reasonable doubt, that he committed crimes, I'm here to tell you, post-traumatic stress syndrome is not an excuse. It's not a defence but it sure might be important in deciding what to do with him if you convict him of something. It sure might be a factor that you ought to consider in assessing punishment. When you look at Mr. Delic as an individual, what do you have? You have a guy that went to high school, got drafted in the army, where he was for a little over 13 months, infantryman, carried a rifle, goes home, gets a job, starts to raise a family, and then he got caught up in a war. When it comes to the purposes of punishment, deterrence, deterrence from a court like this comes two ways. One, the fact that people can be labelled war criminals, just that label itself deters people. Secondly, sentences from courts like this and the post-World War II courts, act to force or to convince policy makers to train people, their soldiers, so they don't commit war crimes, to supervise them so they don't commit war crimes, to set up systems, the list cases, the Von Leeb cases, Nuremberg. I've been to the seminars where senior officers are taught about war crimes. I've taught them. I know what they are told. Just the labelling of a person as a war criminal, fear of that convinces these policy makers, these people that can make the decisions, make the choices, to make the right choices. Retribution, if you want just pure revenge, there's nothing I can say. The Prosecutor seems to think that's an important issue. Punishment for the sake of punishment, I don't think, is very effective, but then I'm a Defence lawyer. Finally, and this is one other thing, on Mr. Landzo's written submission, there are some written statements that are purported to be made by Mr. Delic. I haven't objected to those things coming in, because his counsel has the right to think that those statements may and somehow be mitigating as to Mr. Landzo. If I tried to keep those out, I'd probably be depriving him of his right to effective assistance of counsel. All I ask is if you want to consider them in setting Mr. Landzo's punishment, that's fine with me. I ask you not to consider them in any way, shape, form, or fashion, as they involve Mr. Delic. The Prosecutor recommended sentences on every one of the defendants, and the jurisdiction I'm from, it's allowable. I don't do it with Judges. I figure that Judges are trained, they're experienced, you know what they are doing, and I find that I would be invading your jurisdiction, your job, to tell you what to do. I would just suggest that you think about those factors I've talked about and arrive at a just sentence. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Nancy Boler, and I'm co-counsel for Esad Landzo. Lead counsel Cynthia McMurrey is not present today in Court, but she will be back in court for the verdict. I know that it's probably not proper at this time, but I would just like to say that I think that Tom Moran gave just an excellent argument, closing statement. In addition to what I'm going to say today, I would like to adopt that as well. I echo his sentiments. Let me begin by saying that I'm the mother of a son who's two years older than Esad Landzo was back in 1992. Even without a personality disorder and without a war on his doorstep, I cannot imagine placing the responsibility of guarding 250 or so detainees on someone so young and vulnerable. Esad Landzo had just turned 19 when the war came to Konjic. He was chronically ill and small for his age. You will recall the testimony of the captain in the army, Witness DC-4, who told you about the first time Esad Landzo tried to join the TO. He said that Esad was just a child, and he sent him back home. One of the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the counsel be advised to please slow down just a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: The witness said that the difference in his appearance in the courtroom today and his appearance in 1992 was like night and day. You heard testimony from (name redacted), people from Konjic who knew Esad Landzo when he was young, and from two physicians, Dr. Jajak from Konjic and Dr. Lamers from here in The Hague about his chronic respiratory problems. You heard about frequent hospital visits, beginning when he was just a few months old, and about the home remedies that his mother relied on, such as wearing a pouch on his chest soaked in goat's fat or pig's fat that smelled awful and did little to alleviate his breathing problems. He was a quiet, young man who found happiness with his animals and with his art, and you heard no testimony about violent acts of any kind prior to his experience in the Croatian killing camp or at Celebici. Let me now address some of the arguments from the Prosecution, both today and the written submission. I'd like to echo what Tom Moran just spoke about, in your comments, Ms. McHenry, about turning themselves in. Esad Landzo, too, was the -- my understanding is that his indictment was incorrect also, and it was for a Senad Landzo and not an Esad Landzo, and that this actually went to a Supreme Court there in Sarajevo, and those things just had to be worked out before the authorities could carry out the extradition. So I do just have a quarrel with your assessment that they fought their surrender to The Hague. I just wanted to tell you those facts. I do agree with the Prosecution's statement that Esad Landzo acted under superior orders. We do agree that sometimes he acted under orders, other times, not. He told you that himself in his sworn testimony. Ms. McHenry also stated that he reported that he enjoyed carrying out his orders. Let me just remind the Court that Esad Landzo's early statements to authorities, newspapers, counsellors, therapists, whomever, must be considered in light of his depression at the time and the diminished mental capacity that each mental health expert found independently. I will address the issue of the defence of diminished mental responsibility in just a few minutes. Also, I'd just make a brief comment about the use of the term "long period of time" by Ms. McHenry. I believe that there was presented by the Defence and by some of the Prosecution witnesses that shows that Esad Landzo was there for a maximum of six weeks at Celebici. The comment about an article that we submitted as part of Dr. Goreta's materials, where there were five major criticisms of forensic psychiatry, the first being that psychiatrists always disagree. That may be true most of the time, but in this case, in the case of Esad Landzo, the mental health experts, the psychiatrists, and the psychologists agreed. I'll go along with you on the jargon-ridden testimony, but just to qualify that by saying that medical diagnoses, psychiatric diagnoses are complicated, and it necessitates the use of medical terms and psychiatric terms. So perhaps I would just quarrel with the term "jargon," but certainly agree that it's complicated. There was also mention of an attempt to dictate the law and give conclusive opinions. I believe that we bring mental health experts and that we bring experts of all kinds to the Court, and we hope that the Court seeks guidance from their opinions, not that they were trying to step into shoes that they should not have stepped into. We just believe that that's part of the system. As for Dr. Goreta finding diminished responsibility in all 25 of his subjects and somehow suggesting that it was a faulty study, let me just remind the Court that all 25 of those people were in a mental hospital, a psychiatric hospital, and if you haven't personally been through a psychiatric hospital, it's a tough thing to do. It's a sobering experience. Clearly, those people were very sick to begin with. Ms. McHenry also stated that there was no reason to significantly reduce any sentence because of Mr. Landzo's mental health difficulties. Clearly, this flies in the face of what mitigation evidence is all about and, of course, it's a reason to reduce, significantly, any sentence that the Court may give. I will adopt a word that Ms. McHenry used to characterise some of the Defence arguments that we raised, and I would just have to say that idea is "ludicrous." Of course, it's mitigating evidence. There was also a mention of credit for time spent in Bubulo. We do submit that there ought to be some credit for the co-accused who served time in Bubulo. This event arose directly out of the time that Esad Landzo was at Celebici, arose directly out of events at Celebici, and we ask that the Court just review the relevant information that we attached to our written submission when considering whether or not to give credit for time served for Celebici. Of course, it goes without saying that we also favour and expect that he will get time served for all of the time that he has been in detention here awaiting the end of this trial. As to the written submission, the sentencing submission of the Prosecution, on page 13, the Prosecution states that there should be no mitigation for substantial cooperation with the Prosecution. That's the way they termed it. Ms. McHenry spoke a little bit about that in her oral arguments as well. We disagree and urge the Court to consider the attempts made by Esad Landzo to cooperate with the Prosecution. In his testimony, Esad Landzo, himself, gave evidence regarding this matter, and we ask the Court to accept it as mitigation. We agree with the Prosecution's statement on page 25 as follows: "The Prosecution believes that Landzo's youth and personality problems, including the evidence from the mental health professionals that he was easily influenced, may be considered in fashioning an appropriate sentence." We disagree with the following statement that he represents a continuing danger to society. Professor Van Leeuwen states the opposite in his letter to me, which I received about a week ago, and we submitted it as a written statement in the sentencing phase of this trial. In addition, a review of Dr. Goreta's testimony will also confirm that Esad Landzo has rehabilitated and continues to make further progress in his rehabilitation and is not a danger to society. The Defence of Esad Landzo also objects to the word "blames" in the statement on page 26, wherein the Prosecution states that Landzo blamed his actions on his mental condition, on his youth, on his parents, on his physical health, on his superiors, and on his prior attorney. There's been evidence put forth on each of these matters, and it's clearly relevant evidence as to both guilt, innocence, and to be used in sentencing. Regarding the reference on page 27 to our belief that the prosecution of a camp guard should be a matter for the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina and not for this Tribunal, I'm not going to belabour that point. It's been covered thoroughly in written briefs, but I just must strongly disagree with the Prosecution when they state the following: "Furthermore, such a submission clearly demonstrates the lack of appreciation of or contrition for the pain and misery caused to the victims of his crimes." This is a legal argument, and it just can't follow that by making this legal argument we're demonstrating a lack of appreciation for pain caused to the victims. This is absolutely false. Esad Landzo took the witness stand and admitted his guilt to the crimes that he committed. In his letter to the Court, attached to our submission on sentencing, and in his written statement, he expressed his genuine remorse, his sincere apologies to the victims and their families, and the profound guilty feelings that will stay with Esad Landzo for the rest of his life. Regarding the specifics of sentencing to a certain number of years, I will leave it to what Tom Moran spoke to you about with his witness, Dr. Tomic, a couple days ago, who spoke almost all day about the sentencing practices in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant time in 1992. We would join with the counsel for co-accused that Your Honours, should you choose to sentence the accused to prison, that you do not exceed the 15-year limit in effect in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 at the relevant. In lieu of prison sentences, however, Your Honours have wide flexibility and wide latitude in sentencing, and I just want to urge you to strongly consider alternative sentencing for the co-accused and, specifically, for Esad Landzo. I urge Your Honours that in lieu of prison sentences you also consider probation, probating sentences of five years to ten years probation. That could include electronic monitoring. It could include counselling and therapy. It could include public service, community service, the right of review after each year of probation. Dr. Tomic testified that these types of creative sentencing will become a part of the Bosnian sentencing laws currently being revised. I want to talk for just a moment about the defence of diminished mental responsibility. Let me begin by saying that as early as in her pre-trial brief, Cynthia McMurrey gave notice that she intended to raise the Defence, but when the time came to begin the presentation of the defence of diminished mental responsibility in earnest, we couldn't help but notice, by facial gestures and by body language, the initial scepticism expressed by some of the persons in this courtroom. At this point, what it all boils down to is you believe it or you don't. It's that simple. But, unfortunately, the legal defence of diminished mental responsibility isn't simple at all. It's a complex defence, and our preparation for the presentation of this defence was long and arduous. As you are aware, this is the first time that the defence of diminished mental responsibility was raised in a war crimes trial. However, we brought four mental health experts to testify before you. Although there was some distinction in terminology, each reached the same conclusion independently, that Esad Landzo suffered from a severe personality disorder that amounted to diminished mental capacity. This translates, in legal terms, to diminished mental responsibility for his actions during the relevant time period in 1992. Esad Landzo was unable to exercise his own free will, and my final comment on the defence of diminished mental responsibility is this: We believe that the Defence of Esad Landzo met the burden of proving this special defence of diminished mental responsibility. However, if Your Honours do not so find, then the same evidence must be considered in mitigation. As the Court is aware, this is the practice in numerous jurisdictions throughout the world, and I adopt what Tom Moran said in his mention of post-traumatic stress syndrome, that it is clearly to be considered in mitigation. Only one of the four accused, Esad Landzo, chose to take the witness stand and give sworn testimony. In so doing, he subjected himself to rigorous cross-examination by counsel for the co-accused and by the Prosecution, and he withstood that rigorous cross-examination because he was telling the truth. He was steady and consistent in his testimony because he was telling the truth. He accepted responsibility for the crimes that he was guilty of, and he denied responsibility for the crimes that he was not guilty of. In keeping with the Trial Chamber's request yesterday that we keep these closing remarks brief, I've attempted to do so. After more than 18 months of trial, Your Honours have voluminous amounts of evidence to sort through. In the event of a guilty verdict, I trust that your deliberations will yield a sentence based, not only the negative things submitted by the Prosecution, but also on the positive things submitted by this Defence. As you look at Esad Landzo in the courtroom today, you see a person who has matured in many ways in the six years since Celebici. Certainly, he has matured physically. He was a boy in 1992. Today is a young man. The detention unit is feeding him well. But he has matured emotionally. He has shown his respect for the Court by his manner in the courtroom and even by his choice of courtroom attire, a sports coat, a dress shirt, and a tie. He has matured mentally. With the counselling and the therapy provided by the registry, he has made immense progress in his rehabilitation. I trust that Your Honours will consider all of the evidence before you and that we will come together again in a few weeks to here the results of the hard work that is before you. Let me close by expressing my sincere gratitude to this Registry, to this Trial Chamber, to lead counsel Cynthia McMurrey, and to Esad Landzo for giving me the opportunity to participate in these proceedings. It's been an honour and a privilege. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If you please, Your Honours. One thing that I have always found difficult to comprehend is how it's thought possible that Judges, particularly in multi-defendant and multi-indictment cases, have the mental capacity and ability to determine complex facts with complete discretion, and yet when it comes to the question of sentence, there are people who believe that some sort of judicial, mental block takes place which prevents them from being able to exercise the same form of intellectual discretion as they did with the facts. That's always, I've found, to be one of the great difficulties with those jurisdictions that give such credence to the Prosecution or, indeed, politicians trying to determine what the sentence should be. Judicial independence means just that. It's the intellectual independence of discretion, and I know I am confidant that in this Tribunal that discretion, that independence, will find its prime voice. The idea that deterrence and retribution has not formed part of recent and continuing modern jurisprudence, I find a remarkable assumption. For many years now, the climate of sentencing has changed. In the early part of the Victorian era in the United Kingdom, children were hanged for stealing sheep. That's now regarded as barbaric. As we go through time and we look back in time, it is usually an extended period of time, because jurisprudence moves slowly, slower than political theory in many ways. But as we move on, we see that society has a different view and takes different account of how people act and how they are motivated. One of the principal reasons behind that is there are things like psychology and psychiatry have made great strides, and we are better able now, than we ever were before, to know what motivates people and what makes them tick. Of course, even in allowing for that, there are certain elements of human behaviour which are so distressing, so horrific, that whatever progress is made in one direction, there's a back-surge, in the same way that the tide comes in and out, to prevent ideas taking hold before their time. But their time comes, and modern jurisprudence is moving away from sentencing policy based upon retribution or deterrence, and it's moving into a more enlightened criteria of education and protection. I don't ask that this Tribunal abandon the deterrence and retribution. All I ask is that in that great ambit of discretion, which I started off by saying was the cornerstone of this Tribunal, that that takes its place and takes a prime place in Your Honours' considerations. That's a general point but it's, in my submission, an important general point. I have some more specific points, of course, so far as Mr. Mucic is concerned. Some don't relate, necessarily and exactly, to matters heard in evidence. Of course, questions of guilt or innocence are now historical as far as these submissions are concerned. But they go beyond, perhaps, even questions of sentencing from purely evidential points of view, but I submit that they need to be mentioned. I know, although I wasn't present, that some of the behaviour of Mr. Mucic during these proceedings has caused adverse comment. I know that Your Honours won't take that into account in the great scheme of things, because it doesn't, as it were, emanate from the evidence and isn't part of the decision you have to make, but we would be all less than human if there wasn't some subconscious strata of antipathy to somebody who did not behave properly in a solemn Tribunal. If there is anything in Mr. Mucic's behaviour during the proceedings that has caused you displeasure, all I say is this: That anyone who has suffered long-term incarceration pre-trial and during trial suffers stress, to a greater or lesser degree. It would be disingenuous to suppose one needed to call psychiatric evidence of this, any more than one would need to call medical evidence that it would hurt if you hit yourself over the head with a hammer. It's part of the human condition, and I ask you to take notice that any man, and not a particularly well-educated or sophisticated man, and Mr. Mucic will forgive me for describing him thus, but it's accurate, may suffer the sort of stress and the lapses in personal behaviour which might, otherwise, be the hallmark of a simple man. I also draw to Your Honours' attention the effect of what I call the Bubulo acquittal, which formed part of the addendum to the Defence submissions of Mr. Mucic. Although quite correctly, the Prosecution did not rely upon the allegation that Mr. Mucic was, in any way, involved. Even the mere mention of such involvement raises a shadow of suspicion. In order to completely remove that, the determination of the highest court in Bosnia that Mr. Mucic is acquitted in all respects of any involvement in that is now before the Court to remove that shadow of suspicion. There has been great play made upon the effect before this Tribunal of the persuasive force, because it is only a persuasive force, of the law that pertained in the former Yugoslavia, particularly, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I remind Your Honours respectfully of the evidence of the conjunctive use of the word "and" in Article 33, the importance of a subjective approach to sentencing relating to the individual, and that goes, again, against the objective elements of deterrence and retribution. We heard from Professor Tomic of a fairly sophisticated prisoner regime that was apparent and available in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the war. There were a number of layers of detention from juveniles through adults, in the same way that there are in most societies that have a reasonably sophisticated penal system. Obviously, and I echo the words of my learned friend Mr. Moran here, that if you have such a reasonably sophisticated system, you must have reasonably sophisticated and trained people to run it; otherwise, the system itself is of no avail. It is plain that if you set up a camp, such as Celebici, and turn it in to what, effectively, is a prison, and you then have people brought in, these aren't people who have applied for jobs. These are people who are brought in to run the camp. If they are not people with the sophisticated training, the leadership, the manned management and administration, to look after such a camp, then defects are bound to arise, and people are going to be under pressure. Pressure comes in many ways and many forms. For a simple man, and Mr. Mucic is, I repeat, in many ways, a simple man, to put him in charge of such an institution, if you find that he was so in charge of such an institution, even for a short period of time, is going to be an immense strain upon him. He is not a trained leader. He is not a trained manager. It may well be that in such circumstances, even a mature man, even a physically strong man, seeks to disassociate himself with those responsibilities, perhaps, by the simplest way of all, by simply taking leave, by disappearing, by going away. The whole of the basis of our submissions has to be and the whole of the basis of the Prosecution's submissions at this stage have to be upon the assumption, and, of course, it is only an assumption at the moment, that the Trial Chamber will convict every defendant on each count of the indictment and on the worst possible basis, because it would be irrational to approach it on any other basis. Considering that, of course, the figures put forward by way of suggestion from the Prosecution are based upon that draconian assumption. Of course, therefore, the Trial Chamber will take note of that. First of all, if it takes note of the Prosecution's submission by way of giving a quantum of sentence, it will reduce such quantum in two ways -- I beg your pardon, in three ways. First of all, if people are not convicted on every count of the indictment, there is a pro rata reduction for those matters they are not convicted on. Secondly, if they are not convicted on the worst possible basis, and this is a matter entirely, of course, for judicial discretion, there will be a pro rata reduction for the basis upon which they are convicted. Thirdly, of course, it may well be that the figures put forward by the Prosecution were not, in any event, the figures that the Trial Chamber had in mind, bearing in mind, of course, all the other matters in mitigation, if they be accepted, put forward on behalf of each of the four defendants. That's a critical moment in this case, because the indictment in this case contemplates different bases for different types of convictions for different individuals. It doesn't only allege acts of commission. It alleges acts of omission, and actually says in the particulars of all of the counts that Mr. Mucic faces that he knew or had reason to know whatever it is that is complained of. I take this as an example. If, for any of those counts or, indeed, for all of them, the Trial Chamber is of the view that he is culpable by reason of omission and culpable by reason that he didn't know but that he simply had reason to know that such a thing was happening or such an illegal act was occurring, then that is a hugely different basis upon which to sentence him than someone who deliberately and consciously goes out to commit an offence, regardless of the consequences. I invite you, when sentencing, that if you find that these are acts of omission, and if it's on the basis that he had reason to know, i.e., constructive knowledge rather than actual knowledge, then to approach the sentencing upon that very different basis on each of the counts in the indictment that he faces. You are, and at the risk of sounding, in any way, sycophantic, all experienced and senior judges. It's self-evident that you wouldn't be here if you weren't. I'm not going to go into any sort of detail about the figures that one should approach in sentencing. That would logically fly against what I started off in my submissions, speaking about the widespread discretion, of course, which you have. But it would be amiss of me, bearing in mind that such figures have been suggested by the Prosecution, to ignore it completely. It may be thought that by ignoring them I was somehow concurring in them, and I certainly don't. I mentioned in the written submissions the case of Von Leeb. That's an important case arising out of the Nuremberg trials after the Second World War. Von Leeb was a field marshall. He was in charge of 500.000 men. It was in that area of operations between East Prussia and Moscow in the former Soviet Union, and I have invited Your Honours to take judicial notice of this, that many historians found was an area where the worst of the atrocities, outside of the annihilation of the Jews and other people that took place, the worst of the atrocities were committed by military troops occupying territory. Von Leeb was the head of it. If there was ever a more extreme example of command responsibility, it's difficult to see it. He was convicted on the basis of what was called the Barbarossa jurisdiction order, which was an order which purported to give junior officers the right to shoot people simply because they suspected them of committing offences. He was convicted on the basis that he had passed that order through the chain of command and, therefore, he had criminal responsibility. He was sentenced to three years imprisonment. I refer Your Honours to Article 142 that we dealt with with Professor Tomic. It is plain that, although rather curiously, even when there's a statutory minimum, and I know His Honour Judge Karibi-Whyte, I think, if I'm correct, was slightly taken aback by this, and, indeed, with respect, so was I, that to see there was a statutory minimum and then to find out that it isn't a statutory minimum at all, and, frankly, judges have a discretion to pass a lesser sentence, rather than --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We kindly ask the counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: But there is a statutory minimum nominated, and it's five years. That's regarded as five years strict imprisonment. When I asked that you will recognise, that you will remember, that strict imprisonment related not to the regime but to the amount of imprisonment, the length of imprisonment. In those circumstances, if five years was seen as strict or harsh imprisonment in the former Yugoslavia, that is one benchmark that you can operate from in this case. I don't seek to fetter or suggest any other figure, apart from those I've mentioned, but simply to set them in the scale against the 20-year figure advocated by the Prosecution. Mr. Mucic, his worst offences hitherto are poaching. That indicates, perhaps, that we are dealing with a simple countryman. Those are the sort of offences simple countrymen commit. There is evidence, and it's set out in the written submissions, of him helping other people in the camp. That is powerful mitigation. It is rare, in any case, to have that sort mitigation emanate from Prosecution witnesses, and I know that Your Honours will give it all due consideration when considering sentence, should you convict in this case. If there are any matters which I have not dealt with which you think I should have dealt with, I would invite Your Honours to, perhaps, suggest them to me now. It's a practice we adopt in the United Kingdom, and I can't get away from it. Normally speaking, when a judge says, "I haven't got any questions," it doesn't mean, of course, that the advocate has covered everything. It means that he has gone on for too long. But if there are any such questions or any observations that Your Honours wish to make, I will attempt, to the best of my ability, to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see no reason to make any other suggestions than that. I think you have covered the ground as much as anyone can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for the opportunity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hope that this will be my last address to this Honourable Chamber, because I believe that, after your decision, Zejnil Delalic will no longer need counsel. The closing arguments that we submitted in our written submission addressed a number of issues that were raised in the Prosecutor's submission. Therefore, Your Honours, today I'm not going to dwell on the general matters that we mentioned in our brief having to do with the legal basis for sentencing and the practice in the former Yugoslavia. However, since today, in their final arguments, the Prosecution addressed a number of issues that we expressed in our submission, please allow me to say just a couple of words which are, in my opinion, relevant in the proper determination of the sentence in this case in respect of the accused charged in the indictment of the Celebici case. Both the Defence and the Prosecution agree in their written and oral submissions to the Tribunal that the fundamental principle of anyone's criminal responsibility, and that the basic guidelines, when it comes to determining the appropriate sentence for the accused, has to be the participation of a specific person, of an individual, in the commission of a crime and the basic characteristics of his personality. We, therefore, refer you to these elements and kindly ask you that when it comes assessing the possible responsibility of Zejnil Delalic, to take these elements into account. In their final arguments, the Prosecution has mentioned the gravity of the crime, while dealing with this particular crime in general terms, and also in respect of each of the accused. The gravity of a crime is, by all means, one of the elements that affects the appropriate sentence, and Celebici cannot be any exception to that rule. However, the Prosecutor has criticised today the written submissions by Mr. Delalic and has stated that we have no right to compare ourselves with other serious cases, because this Court only has the evidence that has been presented in the Celebici case. This is contradictory to what the Prosecutor himself has stated in his written submission by referring you to numerous decisions reached at this Tribunal and numerous decisions reached by other International Tribunals. He has done so while discussing the gravity and seriousness of the crimes committed. The Prosecutor has, therefore, quoted the Tadic decision, the Erdemovic judgement, and decisions relating to the Rwanda Tribunal. In their written submission, they even went as far as to claim that the circumstances were identical. I quote, "When the victims of the acts of Dusko Tadic in Kozerac had suffered the horrors of a two day intense shelling and attack on the town which left behind 800 casualties." I know, Your Honours, that you will take into account other judgements and decisions by this Tribunal and other relevant case law. My learned colleague, Mr. Morrison, has reminded you of one of many such decisions. Let me remind you of the already quoted case, the Tadic case, which was cited by the Prosecutor in his submission. He claimed that in two days, 800 people were killed, in Keraterm and that in Srebrenica, within a few days, 8.000 civilians were killed, the civilians who had been under the protection of the United Nations. In the case of Rwanda, 800.000 people were killed. According to the indictment of the Prosecutor, in Celebici, 13 people were killed. Out of that number, and I do not wish to analyse this particular issue, at least six deaths have nothing to do with Celebici. Therefore, I am faced with the question, "Why has the Prosecutor tried, ever since the beginning, to to overemphasise the gravity of the acts that were committed in Celebici?" For me as a human person, any murder is equally serious. For a victim, it is always a tragedy. But remember the first day of our trial, Your Honours, the 10th of March, '97, I reacted very strongly to the comparisons with the Nuremberg trials and the Tokyo trials. I believe that throughout the trial you have reached the same opinion, that is, that these trials have nothing in common. My learned colleague Mr. Moran has spoken about the accused, being charged with the least serious types of war crimes if one can use that legal description. We, here, deal only with grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions. There have been no crimes of genocide or crimes against humanity in this particular case. Therefore, Your Honours, you see that these comparisons are not valid, and you cannot ascribe such gravity, as it is proposed by the Prosecutor, to the case in Celebici. I'm convinced that you will be perfectly able to ascribe appropriate elements to this particular case, the elements that have been established through the evidence that has been presented. I wish to add further comments to what my colleague Mr. Niemann stated today. He said that the circumstances that we offered as important circumstances, namely, the fact that citizens of a particular state had come under aggression, because in the words of my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, it was merely a transitional period. I could not believe my ears, because I had listened to Mr. Niemann in his other addresses before this Honourable Tribunal, when he spoke the same way that I am speaking to you now, that is, that the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a recognised state on the 6th of April, that it was admitted as a member of the United Nations on the 22nd of May, and that it had a legitimate right, as a state and as its citizens, to defend themselves. This, Your Honours, has nothing to do with the rebellion in Prijedor where the civilian population came under attack of those who had rebelled 5 against that state. This, actually, may be the first case in which the defenders or those who had been attacked have been brought before a court. One other important fact that you have in mind is something that was stated by the Prosecution witness, General Divjak, and I will try to quote him. I do not know much about history, and I can tell you that he knows history quite well, but in as much as I know about history, Sarajevo was, by and large, the largest concentration camp after the Second World War. From numerous other witnesses called, both by the Prosecution and the Defence, you have heard that Konjic was the fourth such city in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You have heard about humanitarian tragedy that had befallen this town, the town of Konjic, and I don't think that I need to dwell on this issue any longer. One of the issues that the Prosecutor drew your attention to is that Zejnil Delalic and his Defence did not cooperate with the Prosecutor. He has explained that by the simple fact that Zejnil Delalic had entered a plea of not guilty. According to my reasoning, and I believe this is the reasoning of all lawyers and all courts, that the assistance provided to the Prosecution in reaching the truth and the assistance 5 to provide the Court with all relevant evidence that can be corroborated and its veracity ascertained, is something that amounts to cooperation. An 7 innocent man cannot cooperate with the Prosecution by saying that he's guilty. This would be absurd. In our written submission, we indicated the details of the cooperation of Zejnil Delalic with the Prosecutor. You may know, and you may not know, that Zejnil Delalic and Zdravko Mucic were the only individuals who came to this Tribunal who had been arrested before the Prosecutor issued an indictment against them. Had anyone accused Zejnil Delalic, a man whom you’ve come to know through witness testimonies, as a man who has done something wrong, I'm sure that that person would have come to the Tribunal. Zejnil Delalic gave his first statement on 18 March, the indictment was confirmed on 21st March, and it reached Germany where Zejnil Delalic was arrested on 14 March. Zejnil Delalic informed the Prosecutor by saying that he was ready to answer all his questions, and he spent another two days in August in discussions with the Prosecutor. Zejnil Delalic did not have to provide any evidence to the Prosecutor. He had already given it to the Prosecutor in May, and the Prosecutor used that evidence. On the 27th of May, he suggested that he should make available to the Prosecutor everything that he had in his possession that may amount to evidence. This is considerable and important cooperation. In January, before the Prosecution started presenting its evidence, alongside with two letters, we made available to the Prosecution a number of other documents, and the Prosecutor admitted to this court both orally and in writing, that the Defence of Zejnil Delalic is providing huge amounts of necessary information and evidence. If Mr. Niemann is not aware of that, he may very well ask about that from his learned colleagues Ms. McHenry and Mr. Ostberg, with whom the Defence cooperated over an extensive period of time. This should be labelled as extraordinary contribution of Zejnil Delalic to the determination of the truth in this case. The Prosecutor suggested today that Zejnil Delalic, when he learned about certain things, failed to respond. This is an allegation which cannot be borne by any evidence. In Munich, Zejnil Delalic was perfectly clear. He said that it was the first time that he had heard of such incidents, and he said that he was sorry if such things had, indeed, happened. When he was in Scheveningen, he said, when he heard about desperate individuals who were passing through Konjic and Celebici, he said, and he said this in the presence of relevant authorities at the time, he said, "You must do something to prevent them from doing something wrong." So that was the position of Zejnil Delalic from the beginning. His interviews, and we have heard Bajram Delic, and we have seen the videotape of the interview, the original piece of evidence that was offered by that witness, the answers did not relate to the conditions in the Celebici prison. His answers were in response to a question as to his opinion about the enemy propaganda, that is, the radio and television called Serna. We heard this in evidence, namely, their allegation that 5.000 people were in the tunnel in Bradina, and this was later on denied, and it was proven that nobody was in Bradina at the time. Your Honours, what the Prosecutor wants to say to you about Zejnil Delalic is contradictory to the evidence that is before you. The Prosecutor is saying something about the length, the period of time, over which these crimes were allegedly committed. However, the evidence tells you that Zeljko Klimenta, the last victim in Celebici, and we are talking about the 26th of July, and you know that as of August 10th, hundreds of people were released from Celebici. You know that only 32 of them were later transferred to Musala. This was the last crime before the beginning of August, and you know that there were individual crimes that happened during the night and so on, but I don't want to go into details about that. Zejnil Delalic may have heard something about that from the Red Cross, and he acted promptly. On the 19th, the 24th and 28th of August, he conveyed the orders of the superior command, and he definitely contributed for a positive change of the circumstances. We have evidence that was given by doctors here in this Celebici case. We also have the testimony by General Divjak, who knew about the situation, and the statement made by Zejnil Delalic himself. Therefore, the length and dimensions of the crime, as they have been represented by the Prosecutor, are not founded on evidence that's been presented in this case. The Prosecution further goes on and claims that Zejnil Delalic used the term "Chetnik" when referring to Serbs, but we have heard witnesses who have testified to the opposite. Zejnil Delalic has never, ever referred to Serbs as Chetniks, not even in the evidence that has been mentioned in this regard by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor may not know, and maybe this is not important, but there were, indeed, Chetniks in the Serbian army, and people who refer to themselves as Serbs. Nikola Poplasen , who has recently been elected President 9 of Republika Srpska , commonly referred to himself as a Chetnik,a Chetnik Duke. So does Seselj. and this is not something that he would tell to his friend, to his wife, or to any other Serb. This is something that amounts to an insult, but there are people, again, who, as I said, refer to themselves as Chetniks. Therefore, Your Honours, and I don't think that I need to repeat the testimony, and could not use better words about Zejnil 17 Delalic than our character witnesses, Branko Tomann, an Austrian citizen spoke about him as a person. A Croat, Dako Ruzic,did so. A Serb, Nebojsa did so. A Bosniak, Alija Buturovic, did so. Numerous other Prosecution witnesses, and I'm not going to mention their names now, all of them, even detainees in Celebici, spoke highly of him. You have heard that Zejnil Delalic is a cosmopolitan person, humane person, tolerant person, who has never done anyone any harm and, on the contrary, who has always endeavoured to do only good. What, then, would be Zejnil Delalic's motive to commit any of the crimes with which he has been charged? That he did not have any responsibility in regard to Celebici, that he had no business sitting here for two and a half years, this is something I'm not going to speak about. Your Honours, courts all over the world are faced with the difficult task of reaching verdicts. The Court has to reach a verdict that is either an acquittal or a conviction. This is something that you are bound to do by your duty after you have dutifully examined the evidence which is in front of you in respect of all of the accused, including my client, Zejnil Delalic. Only then, when the Court finds itself ready and brave enough to publicly announce the verdict, only then will my client, Zejnil Delalic, know where he stands. You have lots of experience, Your Honours, and I believe that you will have enough courage, regardless of the pressure to 20 which the International Tribunal has been exposed, and I'm convinced that you will reach a just verdict in this case, and in the case of Zejnil Delalic, I'm sure it is going to be a verdict of acquittal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your submissions. I am happy, as all of you are, that, at long last, we are all making our final submissions in this case. For almost two years now, we have been following through our new Rules, new Rules which are an amalgam of two strange bedfellows, we used to call them, and which is a product of this institution and is unique to it. You've all been following every inch, litigating every point. I'm sure by now you have even lost count of the number of motions you have moved and the number of rulings we have made on the objections in these proceedings. As if this Trial Chamber is jinxed, we still had to go through this particular procedure which we now adopted. If you all remember, we were almost at the end of our proceedings when the Rule relating to sentencing was changed. We have to go back again and find a way to enable you to include your necessary evidence for punishment, as if we would never get out of this trouble. I'm very happy we have found a way, instead of having a pre-sentencing trial, to manage to include a sentencing trial within a provision which could have been done at a time you were collecting evidence for the Defence or for the Prosecution. In fact, my greatest happiness is that without grudging anyone, you all rose to the occasion, wrote the necessary memorandum, and got the necessary witnesses to fit within this period, so that we could comply with the Rules without creating unnecessary problems. On behalf of my colleagues, I thank you very much for your efforts and for the endeavours which you have made to ensure that your clients had the best legal defence anyone can give them. I don't think they could have got anything better than what you have done. It is important in a matter of this nature to do the best for them and then allow the Trial Chamber to do its own side of the exercise. We will try and do our best, and we are hoping that when we deliver our judgement, and it will be an integrated one, it's no longer a judgement and then a sentencing after, it will be integrated in the judgement. We're happy that you have given us every opportunity and every assistance to make sure that we did not fail in the temple of justice. My attitude and I think is that of everyone here, we're only committed to doing justice. It doesn't matter what those outside or those inside think we're doing. It's a matter of conscience, and we do justice to the best of our ability. It is the traditional thing that whoever loses has something else to say about justice, but justice is all we want to do, and that is what, in these circumstances, we are bound to do. Sometimes it is usually thought that after so long a proceeding, taking almost two years, surprisingly this one is so fresh in one's memory, that the two-year period looks like one year or even less. You'll remember everyone's face. You remember the nuances of each of the accused persons. You even remember the witnesses who we heard, because they come in so frequently that you tend to take it as a household thing. We thank you very much for your presentation, which has made everything very clear. Unfortunately, I have no other case to do here, and I'll miss everyone who have argued before this Trial Chamber. I've always had a style of being very taciturn. I don't like interrupting people. I like it to go ahead. If, perhaps, you want to hang yourself, it's all right. It doesn't matter. But I think, generally, I have been very impressed with the advocacy which I have met here. Apart from a few difficult periods, things have worked very well. We thank you very much, and in due course, we will have a notice telling you when the judgement will be delivered. Thank you very much. This Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before you do rise, and I know that I speak for more counsel than one, on the question of the date of the sentencing, plainly, that's an administrative matter. I know that the convenience of counsel does not come high on the list of organising such dates and for good reasons, but I think there are a number of people, for a variety of reasons, who would be pleased if the sentencing procedure was not before the 10th of November. I simply put that figure into the system. If it's impossible, then so be it, but if the sentencing could be after the 10th of November, I know that would make life, administratively, much easier for a number of counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for making your request. I think we will take it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: 5.35 p.m. sine die
